statement:
Determine the ultimate bearing capacity for a rigid strip footing with a rough base having a width Bf = 6 ft and founded at a depth Df = 5 ft. Assume that the footing is concentrically loaded and that the total unit weight below the base of the footing is equal to the total unit weight above the base of the footing, i.e., γ = γa = 125 pcf. The soil has a friction angle φ = 20° and a cohesion c = 500 psf. Assume a general shear condition. First assume that the ground water table is well below the base of the footing and therefore it has no effect on the bearing capacity. Determine the ultimate bearing capacity q_ult in psf.

Use the bearing capacity factors N_c = 14.8, N_q = 6.4 and N_γ = 5.4.

Determine the ultimate bearing capacity for a rigid strip footing with a rough base having a width Bf = 6 ft and founded at a depth Df = 5 ft. Assume that the footing is concentrically loaded and that the total unit weight below the base of the footing is equal to the total unit weight above the base of the footing, i.e., γ = γa = 125 pcf. The soil has a friction angle φ = 20° and a cohesion c = 500 psf. Assume a general shear condition. Assume that the groundwater table is at the base of the footing, i.e., at a depth of 5 ft from the ground surface, so that the effective unit weight (unit weight of water = 62.4 pcf) should be used in the weight term. Determine the ultimate bearing capacity q_ult in psf.

Use the bearing capacity factors N_c = 14.8, N_q = 6.4 and N_γ = 5.4.

A 6 ft × 24 ft footing is founded at a depth of 3 ft below ground elevation with the soil profile and average N160 values as follows: 0 to 3 ft, clayey silt, γt = 115 pcf, N160 = 8; 3 to 6 ft, sandy silt, γt = 125 pcf, N160 = 25; 6 to 11 ft, coarse sand, γt = 120 pcf, N160 = 30; 11 to 36 ft, sandy gravel, γt = 128 pcf, N160 = 68. There is no groundwater. The footing is subjected to an applied stress of 2,000 psf. Use Schmertmann's modified method. The strain influence factor at the base of the footing is IZB = 0.1 for the axisymmetric case (Lf/Bf = 1) and 0.2 for the plane strain case (Lf/Bf ≥ 10); the maximum depth of influence below the base is DI = 2Bf for Lf/Bf = 1 and 4Bf for Lf/Bf > 10; the depth to the peak strain influence factor is DIP = Bf/2 for Lf/Bf = 1 and Bf for Lf/Bf > 10; use linear interpolation between these cases. The peak strain influence factor is IZP = 0.5 + 0.1 (Δp/pop)^0.5, where Δp is the net applied stress at the base of the footing and pop is the effective overburden pressure at the depth of the peak strain influence factor. Take the elastic modulus from the Table 5-16 correlations — sandy silt Es = 4·N160 tsf, coarse sand Es = 10·N160 tsf, sandy gravel Es = 12·N160 tsf — and, because Es is correlated from N160, apply the multiplication factor X (X = 1.25 for Lf/Bf = 1 and 1.75 for Lf/Bf ≥ 10, interpolated linearly) to Es. Divide the influence depth into four layers of thickness 36, 12, 48 and 96 inches with centers at 1.5, 3.5, 6 and 12 ft below the base of the footing. The embedment factor is C1 = 1 − 0.5 (po/Δp), where po is the effective overburden pressure at the base of the footing, and the creep factor is C2 = 1 + 0.2 log10(t/0.1) with t in years. Determine the settlement Si in inches at the end of construction (t = 0.1 yr).

statement: A pile is driven through an upper sand layer and a soft clay layer into a bearing gravel layer. The hydraulic specialist determined that the sand layer is susceptible to scour. The geotechnical specialist determined that the soft clay layer is unsuitable for providing resistance. The shaft resistances are Rs1 = 20 tons in the sand, Rs2 = 20 tons in the soft clay (sensitivity = 4), and Rs3 = 60 tons in the gravel; the toe resistance is Rt = 40 tons. Resistance from the scour susceptible sand layer and the unsuitable soft clay layer cannot be counted toward the ultimate capacity. The soil resistance to driving is the sum of the soil resistances from the scour susceptible and unsuitable layers plus the soil resistance in the suitable support materials, with the driving resistance from the unsuitable clay layer reduced by the sensitivity of the clay. Find the ultimate capacity of the pile, in tons.

A 14 inch square concrete pile is to be driven to a driving capacity of 225 kips. The concrete compressive strength, f′c, is 4,000 psi and the pile prestress, fpe, is 700 psi. For prestressed precast concrete piles the maximum allowable driving stresses are: compressive stress allowed = 0.85 f′c − fpe, and tensile stress allowed (normal environments) = 3 (f′c)^0.5 + fpe, with f′c and fpe in psi. Determine the allowable compressive driving stress, in psi.

A straight-sided drilled shaft with a diameter of 3.0 ft and a depth of penetration of 50 ft supports a vertical design load in a mixed (clay on sand) soil profile: clay from the ground surface to a depth of 32 ft, with sand below. Assume a total unit weight of 125 pcf for clay and 115 pcf for sand. The water table is at a depth of 17 ft (unit weight of water 62.4 pcf). Assume the depth of the zone of seasonal moisture change to be 5 ft. Determine the average effective vertical (overburden) stress σ′v at the mid-depth of the sand layer along the shaft, zi = 41 ft, in tsf.

statement:
Given: Subsurface profile at the abutment is shown in Figure B4-1. Geometry of the abutment is shown in Figure B4-2. Abutment stem is located Bf/3 from the footing toe. Tstem = 1.0 m, TGS = 0.5 m, and Tf = 0.9 m. The height of the abutment, Habut, is 8.5 m, and the length is 25 m. There is no scour potential at this site. Frost penetration depth is 0.6 m (2 ft). Tolerable settlement is 25 mm (1.0 in). Find: Size the footing based on Service Load Design, Group I loads (allowable stress design method), considering both the settlement and bearing capacity. Check for overturning and sliding. [Figure B4-1, Boring B-1: Unit 1a, well-graded sand, 4.5 m thick from the ground surface, γ = 19.6 kN/m³, SPT N-values 14, 18, 25, 28, 25; Unit 1b, well-graded sand (saturated), 1.5 m thick, γ = 19.6 kN/m³, N-values 37, 33; the groundwater table at the top of Unit 1b; Unit 2, shale, 1.5 m shown, γ = 23.5 kN/m³, RQD = 80%, N-values >50. Figure B4-2: abutment of height Habut on a footing of width Bf and thickness Tf; stem of thickness Tstem with the stem and girder seat (width TGS) at its top carrying the superstructure; backfill behind the stem; toe length Dtoe in front.] Loads at the superstructure base per m of wall (Table B4-1), applied through the bearings at the girder seat: dead load D, axial 227 kN/m and shear 41.9 kN/m; live load L, axial 61.6 kN/m and shear 0. Group I factors γ = 1.0 and βD = βL = 1.0; the dead-load shear V = 41.9 kN/m is carried in the loading stages with the superstructure. Initial vertical effective stresses at layer midpoints are measured from the ground surface (Unit 1a midpoint at 2.25 m, Unit 1b midpoint at 5.25 m). Bearing: footing 0.9 m thick with 0.6 m cover, Df = 1.5 m; γw = 9.8 kN/m³; design friction angle φ' = 38° for Unit 1a (from Figures 4-1 and 4-2); Eqn. 5-14 with c = 0, strip footing (sγ = sq = 1.0), level base (bγ = bq = 1.0), dq = 1.0, q = γ Df with γ = 19.6 kN/m³; Nq = 48.9 and Nγ = 78.0 (Table 5-1, φ' = 38°); CWγ = 0.5 + 0.5 Dw/(1.5 Bf + Df) ≤ 1.0 (Eqn. 5-9) and CWq = 0.5 + 0.5 Dw/Df ≤ 1.0 (Eqn. 5-10), with Dw = 4.5 m and the upper-bound width Bf = 6 m for the correction factors; factor of safety 3.0; qult and qall written as a constant plus a coefficient times Bf. Settlement of the sand (shale settlement negligible): 2-on-1 strip distribution Δσv/q = Bf/(Bf + Z) (Figure 5-12) with Z from the footing base to the layer midpoint: Layer 1a from the footing base at 1.5 m to 4.5 m depth (Z = 1.5 m), Layer 1b from 4.5 to 6.0 m depth (Z = 3.75 m); σ'vo at each layer midpoint; Hough method (Eqn. 5-24), ΔH = Ho (1/C′) log[(σ'vo + Δσv)/σ'vo], with C′ = 108 for Layer 1a and C′ = 115 for Layer 1b (Figure 5-19). Footing stability, trial Bf = 5.2 m, per m of wall, moments about the toe: stem centreline at Bf/3 from the toe; the girder seat is 1.8 m high, the stem above it being a 0.5 m thick back wall on the rear half of the stem (centroid at Bf/3 + 0.25 m) and the superstructure load acting on the front half at Bf/3 − 0.25 m; γconcrete = 23.5 kN/m³ and backfill γ = 19.6 kN/m³; soil over the toe (Bf/3 − 0.5 m) wide and 0.6 m deep at its mid-length; soil over the heel (2Bf/3 − 0.5 m) wide with its centroid at 0.5[Bf + (Bf/3 + 0.5 m)]; active pressure PA = ½ Ka γ H² at H/3 with Rankine Ka = tan²(45° − φ′/2), φ' = 38°, taken as 0.24 for design. Stage 1 (abutment built and backfilled, before the superstructure): backfill top at the base of the girder seat, H = 8.5 − 1.8 m; stem weight of the part below the seat, 1.0 m × (8.5 − 1.8 − 0.9) m, at Bf/3; heel soil height 8.5 − 1.8 − 0.9 m. Stage 2 (superstructure erected, before live load): H = 8.5 m; stem area (1.0)(8.5 − 0.9) − (0.5)(1.8) m²; heel soil height 8.5 − 0.9 m; dead load 227 kN/m and shear 41.9 kN/m acting 8.5 − 1.8 = 6.7 m above the footing base. Stage 3 (final): stage 2 plus the live load 61.6 kN/m and the live-load surcharge thrust PLS = Ka γ HLS Habut with HLS = 0.6 m at Habut/2; the surcharge adds only this thrust, no vertical load on the heel. Eccentricity e = Bf/2 − Mtoe/PR, B′f = Bf − 2e (Eqn. 6-6), qapplied = PR/B′f. Sliding: FR = (W + Pv) tan δ (Eqn. 5-38), where W + Pv = PR, the total vertical load used for the eccentricity (stem, footing, soil over the toe and heel, plus the superstructure dead load in stages 2 and 3 and the live load in stage 3) with δ = φ = 38° (footing cast against Unit 1a), passive pressure ignored; the sliding force is PA in stage 1 and PA + V in stages 2 and 3 (the surcharge thrust is not added); FS = FR/Fsliding (Eqn. 5-40). Determine the initial vertical effective stress at the midpoint of the full thickness of Unit 1a (ground surface to 4.5 m depth) and of Unit 1b (4.5 to 6.0 m depth), in kPa.

For the settlement calculation, take σ′vo at the midpoint of each settlement layer, not of each soil unit: layer 1a (1.5 to 4.5 m) at 3.0 m depth, where σ′vo = 58.8 kPa, and layer 1b (4.5 to 6.0 m) at 5.25 m depth.

statement: Figure 10-5 shows the idealized subsurface profile (Step 1), soil properties (Step 3), and trial dimensions of a drilled shaft (Step 4) under consideration for a bridge project. Calculate the nominal side resistance for the two layers of silty sand extending to a depth of 33 ft using the β-method as described above. [Figure 10-5: Layer 1, silty sand (SM) from the ground surface to a depth of 15 ft, N60 = 9, (N1)60 = 14, γ = 115 pcf; groundwater table at a depth of 15 ft; Layer 2, silty sand (SM) from 15 to 33 ft, N60 = 27, (N1)60 = 28, γsat = 125 pcf; Layer 3, stiff clay (CL) from 33 to 60 ft, mean su = 2,000 psf based on lab UU tests, γ = 125 pcf; trial drilled shaft of diameter B = 5 ft extending to a depth of 60 ft.] Illustrative Example 10-5 (Perform Strength Limit State Check for Axial Design): For the trial design presented in Illustrative Example 10-1 and depicted in Figure 10-5, the nominal resistances were calculated in Illustrative Examples 10-1, 10-2 and 10-3. Information provided by the structural engineer includes a governing factored axial load demand corresponding to the Strength I limit state load combination: Σ γQ = 766 kips. Based on the calculated resistances, determine whether the trial design satisfies the LRFD criterion. Use the β-method as applied in the example. For each sand layer: φ' = δ = 27.5 + 9.2 log[(N1)60] (base-10 logarithm, Chen and Kulhawy, 2002); preconsolidation stress σ'p = pa × 0.47 (N60)^m (Eq. 10-11) with m = 0.8 for silty sand and pa = 2,116 psf; OCR = σ'p/σ'v (Eq. 10-9), with σ'v the vertical effective stress at mid-depth of the layer; Ko = (1 − sin φ') OCR^(sin φ') ≤ Kp (Eq. 10-8), with K = Ko (no change of horizontal stress from construction); β = K tan δ (Eq. 10-6); unit side resistance fSN = σ'v β (Eq. 10-7); nominal side resistance of the layer RSN = π B Δz fSN (Eq. 10-5), Δz the layer thickness. Take the unit weight of water as 62.4 pcf. For the Illustrative Example 10-5 check use the resistance factors of Table 8-4: φ = 0.55 for side resistance in cohesionless soil, φ = 0.45 for side resistance in cohesive soil and φ = 0.40 for base resistance in cohesive soil. The clay layer (Layer 3) provides the nominal side resistance RSN,3 = 479.7 kips (Illustrative Example 10-2) and the nominal base resistance RBN,3 = 453.6 kips (Illustrative Example 10-3). The factored resistance is Σ φi Ri = Σ φS,i RSN,i + φB RBN (Eq. 10-2), and the capacity to demand ratio is C/D = Σ φi Ri / Σ γQ. Determine the vertical effective stress σ'v at mid-depth of Layer 1 and of Layer 2, in psf.

statement: Consider the soil profile and trial drilled shaft dimensions of Illustrative Example 10-1. The lower 27 ft of the trial shaft penetrates a stiff clay layer with a mean undrained shear strength of 2,000 psf based on UU triaxial tests performed on Shelby tube samples. Using the α-method presented above, calculate the nominal side resistance provided by the clay stratum represented by Layer 3. Soil profile and trial drilled shaft of Illustrative Example 10-1 (Figure 10-5): Layer 1, silty sand from the ground surface to a depth of 15 ft, γ = 115 pcf; the groundwater table is at a depth of 15 ft; Layer 2, silty sand from 15 to 33 ft, γsat = 125 pcf; Layer 3, stiff clay from 33 to 60 ft, γ = 125 pcf, mean su = 2,000 psf based on lab UU tests. The trial drilled shaft has a diameter B = 5 ft and extends to a depth of 60 ft. Take the unit weight of water as 62.4 pcf. Use the α-method as follows. Convert the UU strength to its equivalent CIUC value by Eq. 10-17, su(UU)/su(CIUC) = 0.911 + 0.499 log[su(UU)/σ'vo], where log is the base-10 logarithm and σ'vo is the vertical effective stress at mid-depth of the clay layer. Then α = 0.30 + 0.17/[su(CIUC)/pa] by Eq. 10-18, with atmospheric pressure pa = 2,116 psf. The unit side resistance is fSN = α su(CIUC), and the nominal side resistance of the layer is RSN = π B L fSN over the clay length L = 27 ft (the full thickness of the clay layer; no length of the shaft is excluded). Determine the vertical effective stress σ'vo at mid-depth of the clay layer (Layer 3), in psf.

statement: Consider the soil profile and trial drilled shaft dimensions of Illustrative Example 10-1. The lower 27 ft of the trial shaft penetrates a stiff clay layer with a mean undrained shear strength of 2,000 psf based on UU triaxial tests performed on Shelby tube samples. Using the α-method presented above, calculate the nominal side resistance provided by the clay stratum represented by Layer 3. Soil profile and trial drilled shaft of Illustrative Example 10-1 (Figure 10-5): Layer 1, silty sand from the ground surface to a depth of 15 ft, γ = 115 pcf; the groundwater table is at a depth of 15 ft; Layer 2, silty sand from 15 to 33 ft, γsat = 125 pcf; Layer 3, stiff clay from 33 to 60 ft, γ = 125 pcf, mean su = 2,000 psf based on lab UU tests. The trial drilled shaft has a diameter B = 5 ft and extends to a depth of 60 ft. Take the unit weight of water as 62.4 pcf. Use the α-method as follows. Convert the UU strength to its equivalent CIUC value by Eq. 10-17, su(UU)/su(CIUC) = 0.911 + 0.499 log[su(UU)/σ'vo], where log is the base-10 logarithm and σ'vo is the vertical effective stress at mid-depth of the clay layer. Then α = 0.30 + 0.17/[su(CIUC)/pa] by Eq. 10-18, with atmospheric pressure pa = 2,116 psf. The unit side resistance is fSN = α su(CIUC), and the nominal side resistance of the layer is RSN = π B L fSN over the clay length L = 27 ft (the full thickness of the clay layer; no length of the shaft is excluded). Determine the nominal side resistance RSN,3 provided by the clay stratum (Layer 3), in kips.

statement: In this example, the trial drilled shaft design introduced as Example 10-1 and used to illustrate calculations of side and base resistance in Examples 10-1, 10-2, 10-3 and 10-5, is checked for Service I Limit State loading conditions. Structural modeling of the superstructure, incorporating the trial foundation design, has been conducted and the factored Service I axial force effects and tolerable settlement provided by the structural engineer are as follows: Service I Limit State: tolerable axial settlement = 1.5 inch under nominal compressive load = 575 kips. Utilize Figure 10-10 as a first-order approximation of the axial load transfer behavior. [Figure 10-5: Layer 1, silty sand (SM) from the ground surface to a depth of 15 ft, N60 = 9, (N1)60 = 14, γ = 115 pcf; groundwater table at a depth of 15 ft; Layer 2, silty sand (SM) from 15 to 33 ft, N60 = 27, (N1)60 = 28, γsat = 125 pcf; Layer 3, stiff clay (CL) from 33 to 60 ft, mean su = 2,000 psf based on lab UU tests, γ = 125 pcf; trial drilled shaft of diameter B = 5 ft extending to a depth of 60 ft.] Use the manual's simple method with Figure 10-10 (Eq. 10-30 and the step-by-step procedure): failure threshold = RSN + RBN = Qc + W, with the nominal resistances from previous examples RSN = 197.2 + 635.6 + 479.7 kips (Layers 1, 2 and 3) and RBN = 453.6 kips. The shaft weight W is computed with a concrete unit weight of 150 pcf over the full 60 ft length, buoyant (150 − 62.4 pcf) below the groundwater table at 15 ft. The normalized displacement is δ/B in percent with B = 60 inches. The axial compressive force Rservice + W equals the normalized axial load (divided by 100 %) times the failure threshold, and Rservice is that force minus W. Chart reading (Figure 10-10, cohesive soil curve, as marked in Figure 10-11): at the normalized tolerable displacement δ/B = 2.5 % the normalized axial load is 93 %. The initial part of the cohesive soil curve is linear from the origin to a normalized force of 50 % at a normalized displacement of 0.40 %. For the expected settlement under the 575-kip Service I load, the axial compressive force is the Service I axial force plus W, the normalized axial force is that force divided by the failure threshold, the normalized displacement is 0.40 % × (normalized axial force in % / 50), and the settlement is the normalized displacement times the shaft diameter. Determine the effective weight W of the trial shaft, in kips.

statement: This example problem demonstrates the strength limit state bearing resistance analyses of an MSE wall with various foundation conditions. A flat bearing surface with and without a high groundwater condition, and a sloping toe without groundwater are examined. The MSE wall configuration to be analyzed is shown in Figure E.2-1 (and in Figure E.1-1). [Figure E.2-1: reinforced zone of height H = 20 ft and reinforcement length L = 18 ft; above the wall face a 2H:1V (1 vertical on 2 horizontal) backslope rises 9 ft to a level surface carrying the traffic surcharge q.] This MSE wall is (assumed to be) a "simple" structure and, therefore, is analyzed with the load factors that typically control external stability analyses (see Figure 4-1). See Example E1 for Steps 1 – 11. However, for these computations, bearing resistances are computed (for several cases) in lieu of defined bearing resistances. Step 2. Establish Project Parameters: Foundation soil, φ'f = 30°, γf = 125 pcf. Factored bearing resistance of foundation soil: for service limit consideration, qnf-ser = 7.5 ksf for 1-inch of total settlement; for strength limit consideration, qnf-str is to be determined. Reinforced wall fill, φ'r = 34°, γr = 125 pcf, pH = 7.3, maximum size ¾-inch. Retained backfill, φ'b = 30°, γb = 125 pcf. Traffic Load: The traffic load is on the level surface of the retained backfill. For external stability, traffic load for walls parallel to traffic and more than 1-ft behind the backface of the MSE wall is represented by an equivalent height of soil, heq equal to 2.0 ft. E2-1: It is not obvious whether the strength or the service (i.e., settlement) limit state controls. Therefore, check both. E2-2 Calculations with groundwater near surface: Compute Strength I (max) limit state bearing resistance and CDR assuming groundwater is 12 ft below the ground surface, as illustrated in Figure E.2-2 (Note: Bf = L′ for MSE wall design). E2-3 Calculations with toe slope and without groundwater: Compute Strength I (max) limit state bearing resistance and CDR assuming with sloping toe and no groundwater, as illustrated in Figure E.2-3, and with the following geometry: B = L − 2 eB = 12.46 ft; b = 4 ft (distance from the wall toe to the slope crest); Df = assume = 0; I = 18.4° (3H:1V). Unfactored loads per lineal foot of wall, from Example E1: FH1 = 18.46 k/lft and FV1 = 4.16 k/lft (thrust of the retained backfill, F1 = ½ γb h² Kab with h = 29 ft, Kab = 0.360, inclined at I = 12.7°); FH2 = 2.55 k/lft and FV2 = 0.57 k/lft (traffic surcharge q = 250 psf); V1 = 45.0 k/lft (reinforced zone, γr H L) and V2 = 10.12 k/lft (sloping fill over the reinforced zone, ½ γr L (h − H)). Moment arms about the centre of the wall base: FH1 at 9.67 ft, FH2 at 14.5 ft, V1 at 0, V2 at 3 ft and FV1 and FV2 at 9 ft (the back of the reinforced zone); FH1 and FH2 overturn, V2, FV1 and FV2 resist. Service limit state: load factors 1.00 on all loads; eccentricity eb-ser = (overturning moments − resisting moments about the base centre)/(V1 + V2 + FV1 + FV2); service bearing stress qv-service = (V1 + V2 + FV1 + FV2)/(L − 2 eb-ser), Meyerhof-type distribution, L = 18 ft. Strength I (max), from Example E1: the factored vertical load on the base is 81.65 k/lft and its eccentricity is eB = 2.77 ft; the factored bearing stress is σV-F = ΣV/(L − 2 eB). Bearing resistance factor φb = 0.65 (Table E2-5.2); factored bearing resistance qR = φb qn (Eq. 4-23); capacity to demand ratio CDR = qR/σV-F. Nominal bearing resistance of the flat base without groundwater by Eq. 4-22 with no embedment term: qn = cf Nc + 0.5 L' γf Nγ, with cf = 0, L' = L − 2 eB and Nγ = 22.4 (Table 4-6, φ'f = 30°). With groundwater (Eq. 4-22 and AASHTO 10.6.3.1.2a-1, no cohesion): qn = 0.5 L' γf Nγ Cwγ, using the moist unit weight γf = 125 pcf; Cwγ from AASHTO Table 10.6.3.1.2a-2: Cwγ = 0.5 at Dw = 0.0 and at Dw = Df, Cwγ = 1.0 at Dw > 1.5 L' + Df (Dw measured from the ground surface in front of the wall), interpolated linearly for intermediate positions of the groundwater table; wall embedment Df = 2 ft. With the sloping toe, Nγ is replaced by Nγq (AASHTO 10.6.3.1.2c): qn = 0.5 L' γf Nγq, with Nγq = 18 read from AASHTO Figure 10.6.3.1.2c-2 for φ'f = 30°, b/B = 0.32 and β = 18.4°. For the service limit state, determine the eccentricity eb-ser at the wall base, in ft, and the service bearing stress qv-service, in ksf.

statement: An example calculation for determining Rndr is illustrated in Equation 7-85 based on the project information provided in Table 7-32. The factored axial load, Q, is 200 kips in compression. Given the site conditions, some resistance will be lost in a soil layer subject to scour. The resistance lost in the scour zone should be determined by an appropriate static analysis method and should not be factored per AASHTO (2014) Article 10.7.3.6. For this example, it is estimated that 50 kips of resistance will be lost in the scour zone. The pile will also be driven into a weathered shale formation that historically has exhibited a loss in toe resistance following initial driving. The resistance lost to relaxation should be factored based the resistance verification method. For this example, it is estimated that 100 kips of toe resistance will be lost. Based on field verification by dynamic testing with signal matching, the resistance loss from relaxation is then 154 kips. The resistance factor for field verification by dynamic testing with signal matching is ϕdyn = 0.65. Compute the nominal resistance by Eq. 7-85, Rn = Q/ϕdyn, and the required nominal driving resistance by Eq. 7-86, Rndr = Rn + Rscour + Rrelax, with the relaxation loss factored as Rrelax = (toe resistance lost)/ϕdyn and the scour loss unfactored. Determine the nominal resistance Rn, in kips.

statement: Determine the factor of safety for a 30 ft high fill slope. The slope angle is 30º. The fill is constructed with soil having the following properties: Total unit weight, γ = 120 pcf; Effective cohesion, c′ = 500 psf; Effective friction angle, φ′ = 20º Use Taylor's chart (Figure 6-14) with the condition FS = Fc = Fφ: for an assumed common factor of safety, compute the developed friction angle by Eq. 6-21, φd = arctan(tan φ′ / Fφ), read Ns for β and φd, and compute the slope height from the inverted Eq. 6-26, H = c′ / (Fc γ Ns). The factor of safety is the common value at which this H equals the actual height. Figure 6-14 readings of the stability number Ns for a slope angle β = 30°, as printed in Examples 6-1 and 6-1a: φd = 20° gives Ns = 0.026; φd = 14°, Ns = 0.055; φd = 12.8°, Ns = 0.065; φd = 10.8°, Ns = 0.073; φd = 10°, Ns = 0.075; φd = 8°, Ns = 0.087. Interpolate linearly between these readings. For an assumed common factor of safety Fc = Fφ = 1.6, determine the slope height H given by Eq. 6-26, in ft.

statement: Figure 6-20 shows a 35 ft high slope with a grade of 1.5H:1V. The soil properties within the slope and under it are shown on the figure. Groundwater is immediately under the slope. Calculate the factor of safety for a toe circle by using total stress analysis based on the soil properties shown. (Note: The circle in Figure 6-20 is plotted in Step 5 of the solution.) Figure 6-20 (Data for Example 6-2): within the 35 ft slope, γt = 120 pcf, φu = 20º, cu = 500 psf; the foundation layer below the toe, 25 ft thick, γt = 120 pcf, φu = 0º, cu = 1,000 psf; the water table is at the level of the toe. The plotted toe circle subtends δ1 = 54º within the slope and δ2 = 29º within the foundation. Use Janbu's charts (Figure 6-19) for a toe circle. There is no tension crack, no surcharge on the slope, no water above the toe and no seepage out of the slope, so the correction factors μt, μq, μw and μ′w are all 1.0. Pd = (γH + q − γwHw)/(μt μq μw) by Eq. 6-27 and Pe = (γH + q − γwH′w)/(μq μ′w) by Eq. 6-29. λCφ = Pe tanφ / c by Eq. 6-30; for the first estimate take the strength of the soil within the slope height. Then average the strength along the circle in proportion to the subtended angles, cav = (δ1 c1 + δ2 c2)/(δ1 + δ2) and tan φav = (δ1 tan φ1 + δ2 tan φ2)/(δ1 + δ2), recompute λCφ with cav and tan φav, and compute FS = Ncf cav / Pd (Eq. 6-31). From Figure 6-19, the critical stability number is Ncf = 10.0 for b = 1.5 and λCφ = 1.5. Determine the driving pressure Pd, in psf.

statement: Figure 6-20 shows a 35 ft high slope with a grade of 1.5H:1V. The soil properties within the slope and under it are shown on the figure. Groundwater is immediately under the slope. Calculate the factor of safety for a toe circle by using total stress analysis based on the soil properties shown. (Note: The circle in Figure 6-20 is plotted in Step 5 of the solution.) Figure 6-20 (Data for Example 6-2): within the 35 ft slope, γt = 120 pcf, φu = 20º, cu = 500 psf; the foundation layer below the toe, 25 ft thick, γt = 120 pcf, φu = 0º, cu = 1,000 psf; the water table is at the level of the toe. The plotted toe circle subtends δ1 = 54º within the slope and δ2 = 29º within the foundation. Use Janbu's charts (Figure 6-19) for a toe circle. There is no tension crack, no surcharge on the slope, no water above the toe and no seepage out of the slope, so the correction factors μt, μq, μw and μ′w are all 1.0. Pd = (γH + q − γwHw)/(μt μq μw) by Eq. 6-27 and Pe = (γH + q − γwH′w)/(μq μ′w) by Eq. 6-29. λCφ = Pe tanφ / c by Eq. 6-30; for the first estimate take the strength of the soil within the slope height. Then average the strength along the circle in proportion to the subtended angles, cav = (δ1 c1 + δ2 c2)/(δ1 + δ2) and tan φav = (δ1 tan φ1 + δ2 tan φ2)/(δ1 + δ2), recompute λCφ with cav and tan φav, and compute FS = Ncf cav / Pd (Eq. 6-31). From Figure 6-19, the critical stability number is Ncf = 10.0 for b = 1.5 and λCφ = 1.5. Determine the factor of safety FS of the toe circle (dimensionless).

statement: Find the safety factor for the 20 ft high embankment illustrated in Figure 6-23 by using the simple sliding block method and Rankine earth pressure coefficients. Consider a 1 ft wide strip of the embankment into the plane of the paper. Figure 6-23: a 20′ embankment with a 2H:1V slope, γt = 110 pcf, φ = 30°, on a 10′ layer with γt = 110 pcf, φ = 30°, over a 1′ soft clay layer c = 400 psf on firm material; the water table is at the top of the soft clay layer. The active wedge extends from the embankment top down to the clay (dashed lines), the central block lies between the vertical lines through the crest and the toe of the slope, and the passive wedge extends from the ground surface at the toe down to the clay. Use the simple sliding block method with Rankine coefficients: Ka = tan²(45 − φ/2), Kp = tan²(45 + φ/2); active driving force Pa = ½ γt H² Ka over the full height from the embankment top to the top of the clay (Eq. 6-34), using γt as the water table is below the failure plane; central block resistance cl = cohesion of the clay times the base length of the central block between the verticals through crest and toe; passive resisting force Pp = ½ γt H² Kp over the height from the toe ground surface to the top of the clay (Eq. 6-35); safety factor = (cl + Pp)/Pa (Eq. 6-33). Determine the Rankine active earth pressure coefficient Ka (dimensionless).

statement: For the geometry shown in the following figure, determine the settlement at the center of a wide embankment placed on a silty sand layer by using Modified Hough method and the po diagram. Figure: an embankment 20 ft high with γt = 120 pcf on a 10 ft layer of silty sand with γt = 120 pcf and N160 = 20. Use the Modified Hough method, Eq. 7-1: ΔH = H (1/C′) log10[(po + Δp)/po], with the silty sand layer taken as one layer of thickness H = 10 ft and po and Δp evaluated at its center. The embankment is wide, so the stress increase does not dissipate with depth (Δp equals the embankment pressure γt × height). No groundwater is shown; use total unit weights. From Figure 7-7, the bearing capacity index for the silty sand curve at N160 = 20 is C′ ≈ 58. Determine the original overburden pressure po at the center of the silty sand layer, in psf.

statement: Determine the magnitude of and the time for 90% consolidation for the primary settlement of a “wide” embankment by using the po diagram. Figure: an embankment 20′ high with γt = 120 pcf on a 10′ layer of clay (normally consolidated), γt = 120 pcf, Cc = 0.5, eo = 1.0, cv = 0.2 ft²/day, underlain by rock. The po diagram shows po = 600 psf and Δp = 2,400 (pf = 3,000) at a depth of 5 ft, the center of the clay. Since the embankment is wide, the vertical stress at its base is the same within the 10 ft clay layer. Use Eq. 7-2 for the normally consolidated clay, ΔH = H [Cc/(1 + eo)] log10[(po + Δp)/po], with the layer taken as one layer at its center. For the time, use Eq. 7-8, t = T Hd²/cv, with Tv = 0.848 for 90 % consolidation from Table 7-4 and single vertical drainage, because the rock under the clay is impervious (drainage path Hd = full clay thickness). Determine the primary consolidation settlement ΔH of the clay layer, in ft.

statement: For example, the factor of safety for the proposed embankment illustrated in Figure 6-6 can be computed as follows: Figure 6-6 (Example proposed embankment): a fill 30 ft high, γFill = 130 pcf, placed on soft clay with C = 1100 psf, underlain by a firm base. Use the simple rule of thumb of Eq. 6-13 for a preliminary factor of safety against circular arc failure of an embankment on a clay foundation without free water: FS ≅ 6 c / (γFill × HFill), where c is the unit cohesion of the clay foundation soil (psf), γFill the unit weight of the fill (pcf) and HFill the height of the fill (ft). Determine the rule-of-thumb factor of safety FS of the embankment against circular arc failure (dimensionless).

statement: Construct the lateral pressure diagram due to a line load of 700 lb/ft located 15 ft behind the top of a 30 ft high unyielding wall shown below. (Geometry of the Example Problem 10-2: a vertical wall 30 ft high retaining level ground; the line load Ql = 700 lb/ft acts on the ground surface at a horizontal distance of 15 ft behind the top of the wall.) Use the line-load solution of Figure 10-14 (Boussinesq equation modified by experiment, unyielding wall), with m = x/H, where x is the horizontal distance from the wall to the line load, and n = z/H, where z is the depth below the top of the wall and H the wall height. For m ≤ 0.4: Ph (H/Ql) = 0.20 n / (0.16 + n²)². For m > 0.4: Ph (H/Ql) = 1.28 m² n / (m² + n²)². Ph is the lateral pressure on the wall at depth z. Determine the lateral pressure Ph on the wall at a depth of 3 ft below the top of the wall (n = z/H = 0.1), in psf.

(Geometry of the Example Problem 10-2: a vertical wall 30 ft high retaining level ground; the line load Ql = 700 lb/ft acts on the ground surface at a horizontal distance of 15 ft behind the top of the wall.) Use the line-load solution of Figure 10-14 (Boussinesq equation modified by experiment, unyielding wall), with m = x/H, where x is the horizontal distance from the wall to the line load, and n = z/H, where z is the depth below the top of the wall and H the wall height. For m ≤ 0.4: Ph (H/Ql) = 0.20 n / (0.16 + n²)². For m > 0.4: Ph (H/Ql) = 1.28 m² n / (m² + n²)². Ph is the lateral pressure on the wall at depth z. Determine the lateral pressure Ph on the wall at a depth of 24 ft below the top of the wall (n = z/H = 0.8), in psf.

statement: Determine the ultimate geotechnical pile capacity, Qu, for the 1 sq ft precast concrete pile. (Sketch: the pile is embedded 40 ft in silty sand, γ′ = 62.5 pcf, φ = 30°, c = 0, with the water table at the ground surface.) Since ω = 0, use Equation 9-5: Qu = Kδ CF pd sin δ Cd D + At αt pt N′q, where the following terms are known from the problem: At = 1 sq.ft; pt = 40 γ′ = 2,500 psf; pd = 20 γ′ = 1,250 psf; ω = 0°, D = 40 ft, Cd = 4 ft. Use the Nordlund method: shaft resistance Rs = Kδ CF pd sin δ Cd D (Equation 9-6); toe resistance Rt = At αt pt N′q (Equation 9-7a), limited to Rt = qL At (Equation 9-7b), the smaller governing; Qu = Rs + Rt. Chart values as read in the example: δ/φ = 0.76 (Figure 9-7, V = 1 ft3/ft, curve c for precast concrete piles); Kδ = 1.15 (Figure 9-9, ω = 0, V = 1 ft3/ft); CF = 0.9 (Figure 9-12, δ/φ = 0.76); N′q = 30 and αt = 0.5 (Figure 9-13(b), φ = 30°, D/B = 40); limiting unit toe resistance qL ≈ 10 ksf (Figure 9-14). Take 1 ton = 2,000 lbs. Determine the shaft resistance Rs of the pile, in tons.

statement: Given: The proposed embankment geometry as shown in Figure A.5-2 and the embankment and foundation soil properties at the east approach as provided in Table A.5-1. Assume that the shallow (≈ 3′) surface layer of organic material shown in the idealized soil profile (Figure A.4-2) has been removed and replaced with select material having the same properties as the embankment fill. Required: Perform hand calculations based on the Ordinary Method of Slices to compute the minimum factor of safety of the I-0 approach embankment at the east abutment. Compare the minimum factor of safety obtained from the hand calculations with the minimum factors of safety obtained from computer analyses based on the Ordinary Method of Slices and Bishop's Method. Perform hand calculations based on the sliding (Rankine) block method to compute the minimum factor of safety of the I-0 approach embankment at the east abutment and compare the result with the results obtained from the two circular arc type failure analyses. Determine critical failure mode. Perform hand calculations to assess the potential for lateral squeeze of the embankment foundation soils at this location. Table A.5-1, Geotechnical engineering properties of embankment and foundation soils, East Abutment (Boring BAF-4): Embankment fill: c = 0 psf, φ′ = 40°, γt = 130 pcf. Sand: c = 0 psf, φ′ = 36°, γt = 110 pcf, γsat = 110 pcf, γb = 50 pcf. Silty clay: c = 1,100 psf, φ′ = 0, γt = 125 pcf, γsat = 125 pcf, γb = 65 pcf. Gravel: c = 0 psf, φ′ = 43°, γt = 130 pcf, γsat = 130 pcf, γb = 70 pcf. Figure A.5-2 (Idealized design soil profile, East Abutment): a 33 ft high fill embankment with a 2:1 side slope rests on a 7 ft sand layer, underlain by 35 ft of clay over dense gravel; beyond the toe of the slope the ground surface is 10 ft above the top of the clay, and the clay thins to 25 ft at the left edge of the section; the water table lies within the sand layer. Trial failure circle for the hand solution (the center and radius are those of the minimum-FS circle of the computer solution by Bishop's Method). The soil mass above the arc is divided into 16 vertical slices, numbered from the embankment crest (Slice 1) to the toe side (Slice 16). For each slice the thickness of each stratum is given at the two vertical sides of the slice (one value when equal at both sides); the slice weight per foot of length uses the mean of the two side heights times the width. α is the angle at the circle center between the vertical and the radius to the middle of the slice base (positive on the crest side); l is the chord length of the slice base used in place of the arc length. Slice 1: width 15 ft; fill (130 pcf) 33 ft at one side tapering to 0 ft; α = +60°, chord length l = 36 ft; base in fill, c = 0, φ = 40°, pore water pressure u = 0 psf. Slice 2: width 2 ft; fill (130 pcf) 33 ft; sand (110 pcf) 2 ft tapering to 0 ft; α = +54°, chord length l = 3 ft; base in sand, c = 0, φ = 36°, pore water pressure u = 0 psf. Slice 3: width 4 ft; fill (130 pcf) 33 ft; sand (110 pcf) 7 ft and 2 ft at the two sides; α = +51°, chord length l = 7 ft; base in sand, c = 0, φ = 36°, pore water pressure u = 150 psf. Slice 4: width 12 ft; fill (130 pcf) 33 ft; sand (110 pcf) 7 ft; clay (125 pcf) 12 ft tapering to 0 ft; α = +43°, chord length l = 17 ft; base in clay (c = 1,100 psf, φ = 0; total stress, pore pressure not used). Slice 5: width 12 ft; fill (130 pcf) 33 ft; sand (110 pcf) 7 ft; clay (125 pcf) 19 ft and 12 ft; α = +34°, chord length l = 15 ft; base in clay (c = 1,100 psf, φ = 0; total stress, pore pressure not used). Slice 6: width 12 ft; fill (130 pcf) 33 ft; sand (110 pcf) 7 ft; clay (125 pcf) 25 ft and 19 ft; α = +25°, chord length l = 15 ft; base in clay (c = 1,100 psf, φ = 0; total stress, pore pressure not used). Slice 7: width 12 ft; fill (130 pcf) 27 ft and 33 ft; sand (110 pcf) 7 ft; clay (125 pcf) 25 ft and 28 ft; α = +16°, chord length l = 13 ft; base in clay (c = 1,100 psf, φ = 0; total stress, pore pressure not used). Slice 8: width 12 ft; fill (130 pcf) 20 ft and 27 ft; sand (110 pcf) 7 ft; clay (125 pcf) 30 ft and 28 ft; α = +9°, chord length l = 13 ft; base in clay (c = 1,100 psf, φ = 0; total stress, pore pressure not used). Slice 9: width 12 ft; fill (130 pcf) 14 ft and 20 ft; sand (110 pcf) 7 ft; clay (125 pcf) 30 ft; α = +1°, chord length l = 12 ft; base in clay (c = 1,100 psf, φ = 0; total stress, pore pressure not used). Slice 10: width 12 ft; fill (130 pcf) 9 ft and 14 ft; sand (110 pcf) 7 ft; clay (125 pcf) 28 ft and 30 ft; α = −7°, chord length l = 12 ft; base in clay (c = 1,100 psf, φ = 0; total stress, pore pressure not used). Slice 11: width 12 ft; fill (130 pcf) 9 ft and 3 ft; sand (110 pcf) 7 ft; clay (125 pcf) 25 ft and 28 ft; α = −15°, chord length l = 13 ft; base in clay (c = 1,100 psf, φ = 0; total stress, pore pressure not used). Slice 12: width 13 ft; soil at 110 pcf 10 ft; clay (125 pcf) 19 ft and 25 ft; α = −24°, chord length l = 14 ft; base in clay (c = 1,100 psf, φ = 0; total stress, pore pressure not used). Slice 13: width 12 ft; soil at 110 pcf 10 ft; clay (125 pcf) 12 ft and 19 ft; α = −32°, chord length l = 14 ft; base in clay (c = 1,100 psf, φ = 0; total stress, pore pressure not used). Slice 14: width 12 ft; soil at 110 pcf 10 ft; clay (125 pcf) 12 ft tapering to 0 ft; α = −42°, chord length l = 16 ft; base in clay (c = 1,100 psf, φ = 0; total stress, pore pressure not used). Slice 15: width 4 ft; sand (110 pcf) 10 ft and 5 ft at the two sides; α = −49°, chord length l = 6.5 ft; base in sand, c = 0, φ = 36°, pore water pressure u = 150 psf. Slice 16: width 4 ft; sand (110 pcf) 5 ft tapering to 0 ft; α = −53°, chord length l = 6.5 ft; base in sand, c = 0, φ = 36°, pore water pressure u = 0 psf. Use the Ordinary Method of Slices (hand solution) for a unit thickness into the plane of the paper: T = WT sin α (driving), N′ = WT cos α − u l, frictional resistance N′ tan φ, cohesive resistance c l, and FS = [Σ N′ tan φ + Σ c l] / Σ WT sin α (Equations 6-14 to 6-20). Sliding block trial (Figure A.5-11): Rankine active wedge behind the embankment crest through the 33 ft of fill (γt = 130 pcf, φ = 40°) and the 7 ft of sand (γt = 110 pcf, φ = 36°) down to the top of the clay; under the embankment the water table is 2 ft below the top of the sand, so 2 ft of sand lies above it and 5 ft below it. Rankine passive wedge beyond the toe in 10 ft of sand (γt = 110 pcf, φ = 36°), with the water table 5 ft below the ground surface (5 ft above, 5 ft below). Below the water table use the buoyant unit weight of the sand, γb = 50 pcf. The central block slides on the top of the clay (c = 1,100 psf) over a length L = 60 ft. Use Rankine coefficients Ka = tan²(45° − φ/2) and Kp = tan²(45° + φ/2); compute pressures and forces in kips (1 kip = 1,000 lbs) for a unit thickness; FS = (Pp + cL) / Pa. For Slice 15, determine the total weight WT, the tangential driving force T, the effective normal force N′ = WT cos α − u l and the frictional resistance N′ tan φ, in lbs.

Given: The footing geometry and subsurface conditions shown in Figure A.7-2 for the center pier of the Apple Freeway Bridge. The results of Standard Penetration tests (SPT-N blow counts) performed in Boring BAF – 2 as shown in Figure A.7-2. The footing geometry and subsurface conditions shown in Figure A.6-2 for the east embankment of the Apple Freeway Bridge. Values of relevant soil as provided in the previous example (Refer to Section A.6). Required: Compute the ultimate bearing capacity of a rectangular footing at the pier location and apply an appropriate factor of safety to obtain the allowable bearing pressure. Compute the pressure transmitted to the underlying clay layer by the footing and compare that pressure to the allowable clay bearing capacity. Compute the magnitudes of the anticipated immediate and consolidation settlement due to the rectangular footing at the pier location. Compute the ultimate bearing capacity of a rectangular footing founded within the embankment at the East Abutment and apply an appropriate factor of safety to obtain the allowable bearing pressure. Compute the magnitudes of the anticipated immediate and consolidation settlement due to the rectangular footing founded within the embankment at the East Abutment. Taking into account pretreatment by wick drains (Refer to Section A.6-5). Compute the time required for the settlement of the footing to occur. Take into account pretreatment by wick drains and continuing consolidation due to the embankment fill. Plot settlement-time curves for both the pier and embankment footings. Figure A7-2 (Footing geometry and subsurface conditions for center pier of the Apple Freeway Bridge including SPT-N blow counts from Boring BAF-2): a 7 ft wide pier footing with its base 4 ft below the ground surface, in sand; the water table is 10 ft below the ground surface; the sand extends to 15 ft below the ground surface, over clay; SPT-N blow counts in BAF-2, from the top down: 4, 6, 11, 21, 22, 40, 37, 33. Pier footing geometry: embedment below final grade Df = 4 ft; width Bf = 7 ft; length Lf = 100 ft; depth to ground water below the base of the footing Dw = 6 ft. Since Lf/Bf > 10 the footing is treated as continuous. Sand: γt = 110 pcf, internal friction angle φ ≈ 36° (estimated from the average corrected blow count N160 = 36 with Table 8-3), c = 0. Use Equation 8-6 with c = 0: qult = q Nq CWq sq bq dq + 0.5 γ Bf Nγ CWγ sγ bγ, with surcharge q = γt Df and the factors as applied in the example: Nq = 37.8, Nγ = 56.3 (Table 8-1, φ = 36°); sq = 1.05, sγ = 0.97 (Table 8-4); bq = bγ = 1.0 (horizontal base); CWq = 1.0, CWγ = 0.786 (Table 8-5, water table within 1.5Bf below the base); dq ≈ 1.15 (Table 8-6, Df/Bf = 0.57). Allowable bearing capacity qall = qult / FS with FS = 3. Pressure transmitted to the clay: spread the allowable footing pressure qall at 2:1 across the footing width only (strip), down to the top of the clay 11 ft below the footing base: pclay = qall Bf / (Bf + 11 ft). Determine the surcharge term and the unit-weight term of the bearing capacity equation and the ultimate bearing capacity qult of the pier footing, in psf.

Apply the stated shape factors although the footing is treated as continuous.

statement: Figure 14(b), Example Calculations for Dynamic Loading on Walls. Case 1 - Vertical wall with horizontal backfill: H = 20', φ = 35°, γ = 120 PCF, Kh = 0.2, Kv = 0. Combined effect of static and dynamic force: PAE = F1 + F2. Case 2 - Sloping wall with sloping backfill: height 20', φ = 35°, γ = 120 PCF, Kh = 0.2, Kv = .05; the back of the wall is inclined at θ = 10° from the vertical and the backfill slopes at β = 15°. Assume a smooth wall, δ = 0. Case 1: the static force is F1 = 1/2 γH² KA, with the Rankine coefficient KA = tan²(45° − φ/2) of Figure 2, acting at H/3 above the base of the wall; the dynamic increment is F2 = 3/8 γH² Kh, acting at 0.6H above the base of the wall. Case 2: the combined active force is PAE = 1/2 γH² KA(β*, θ*)(1 − Kv) F, where ψ = tan⁻¹[Kh/(1 − Kv)], β* = β + ψ (modified slope of backfill), θ* = θ + ψ (modified slope of wall back) and F = cos²θ*/(cos ψ cos²θ) (the factor F of Figure 14(a)). KA(β*, θ*) and the static KA(β, θ) both come from the Coulomb equation of Figure 8: KA = cos²(φ − θ) / {cos²θ cos(θ + δ) [1 + √(sin(φ + δ) sin(φ − β) / (cos(θ + δ) cos(θ − β)))]²}. The static force is PA = 1/2 γH² KA(β, θ) and the dynamic increment is ΔPE = PAE − PA. Determine the static active earth pressure coefficient KA for Case 1 (dimensionless).

statement: Figure 21, Example of Analysis of Anchored Bulkhead. A sheet pile bulkhead is restrained by an anchor (tie rod) 6 ft below the top of the backfill (point A). Surcharges on the backfill: a uniform q = 300 PSF and a line load QL = 5,000 PLF at 3 ft from the wall. Upper soil, from the top (A) to point C 24 ft below the top: φ1 = 25°, c1 = 100 PSF, γT = 115 PCF. Lower soil, below C: φ2 = 35°, c2 = 50 PSF, γT = 130 PCF. The water level behind the wall is 5 ft below the top (point B); the outside water level is 2.5 ft lower. The dredge line (point D) is 6 ft below C, so H = 30 ft, and the sheeting toe (point E) is 14 ft below the dredge line. Moment reduction: assume fs = 27,000 PSI, E = 30,000,000 PSI; try ZP 32, I = 385.7 IN⁴, S = 38.3 IN³. Values read in the example: KA = .41 for the upper soil and KA = .27 for the lower soil (Figure 3); Kp = 6.0 for the lower soil (Figure 5); wall friction δ = 14° (Table 1); line-load resultant PH = 0.55 QL (Figure 11, m = x/H = 0.1) acting at R = 0.60H above the dredge line; and, for the trial section, Mdesign/Mmax = 0.83 (Figure 19). Active pressure including the uniform surcharge: σH = σv KA − 2c√KA (Figure 2), negative values taken as zero; passive pressure σH = γz Kp + 2c√Kp. Below the water the example uses submerged unit weights of .053 KCF (upper soil) and .068 KCF (lower soil), with γw = .0625 KCF; the net water pressure is γw × 2.5 ft. Safety factor against toe failure: take moments about the anchor A, Fs = Σ moments of passive forces / Σ moments of active forces. Anchor pull: Ap = ΣPA − ΣPp/Fs with Fs = 2.5. Maximum bending moment at the point of zero shear, located at depth X below the outside water level. Moment reduction by Rowe's flexibility number ρ = (H + D)⁴/(EI), with H + D in inches (Figure 19). Resultant forces as labelled in Figure 21, with their lever arms about the anchor A used in the safety factor: PA1 = 1.55 KIP (0.73 ft), PH = 2.75 KIP (6 ft), PA2 = 10.4 KIP (10.52 ft), PA3 = 4.05 KIP (21.09 ft), PA4 = 10.9 KIP (31.0 ft), Pp1 = 43.26 KIP (33.3 ft). In the bending-moment computation the example places PA1 2.1 ft above the outside water level. Anchor pull: ΣPA = PA1 + PH + PA2 + PA3 + PA4 (all five labelled active forces, the line-load resultant PH included; the net water pressure is part of the labelled forces and is not added separately) and ΣPp = Pp1. Point of zero shear: at depth X below the outside water level the shear is Ap − PA1 − PH − (resultant of the net pressure between the outside water level and X) = 0, where PA1 stands for all pressure above the outside water level, PH (12 ft deep, 4.5 ft below the outside water level) lies above X, and the net pressure below the outside water level is the active pressure of the upper soil plus the constant net water pressure γw × 2.5 ft. Mmax is the moment of these same loads (Ap, PA1, PH and the net pressure above X) about the point of zero shear. Determine the active earth pressure σH at point B (5 ft below the top), in ksf.

The water level behind the wall is 5 ft below the top (point B); the outside water level is 2.5 ft lower. The dredge line (point D) is 6 ft below C, so H = 30 ft, and the sheeting toe (point E) is 14 ft below the dredge line. Moment reduction: assume fs = 27,000 PSI, E = 30,000,000 PSI; try ZP 32, I = 385.7 IN⁴, S = 38.3 IN³. Values read in the example: KA = .41 for the upper soil and KA = .27 for the lower soil (Figure 3); Kp = 6.0 for the lower soil (Figure 5); wall friction δ = 14° (Table 1); line-load resultant PH = 0.55 QL (Figure 11, m = x/H = 0.1) acting at R = 0.60H above the dredge line; and, for the trial section, Mdesign/Mmax = 0.83 (Figure 19). Active pressure including the uniform surcharge: σH = σv KA − 2c√KA (Figure 2), negative values taken as zero; passive pressure σH = γz Kp + 2c√Kp. Below the water the example uses submerged unit weights of .053 KCF (upper soil) and .068 KCF (lower soil), with γw = .0625 KCF; the net water pressure is γw × 2.5 ft. Safety factor against toe failure: take moments about the anchor A, Fs = Σ moments of passive forces / Σ moments of active forces. Anchor pull: Ap = ΣPA − ΣPp/Fs with Fs = 2.5. Maximum bending moment at the point of zero shear, located at depth X below the outside water level. Moment reduction by Rowe's flexibility number ρ = (H + D)⁴/(EI), with H + D in inches (Figure 19). Resultant forces as labelled in Figure 21, with their lever arms about the anchor A used in the safety factor: PA1 = 1.55 KIP (0.73 ft), PH = 2.75 KIP (6 ft), PA2 = 10.4 KIP (10.52 ft), PA3 = 4.05 KIP (21.09 ft), PA4 = 10.9 KIP (31.0 ft), Pp1 = 43.26 KIP (33.3 ft). In the bending-moment computation the example places PA1 2.1 ft above the outside water level. Anchor pull: ΣPA = PA1 + PH + PA2 + PA3 + PA4 (all five labelled active forces, the line-load resultant PH included; the net water pressure is part of the labelled forces and is not added separately) and ΣPp = Pp1. Point of zero shear: at depth X below the outside water level the shear is Ap − PA1 − PH − (resultant of the net pressure between the outside water level and X) = 0, where PA1 stands for all pressure above the outside water level, PH (12 ft deep, 4.5 ft below the outside water level) lies above X, and the net pressure below the outside water level is the active pressure of the upper soil plus the constant net water pressure γw × 2.5 ft. Mmax is the moment of these same loads (Ap, PA1, PH and the net pressure above X) about the point of zero shear. Determine the design moment Mdesign, in ft-kips, and the computed bending stress Mdesign/S in the trial section ZP 32, in psi.

statement: Figure 8, Example Problem - Batter Pile Group as Guy Anchorage. A guy pull P = 90 K, inclined at α above the horizontal, acts on a pile cap whose base is at EL-3. Soil profile: EL-0 ground surface; firm sand, γT = 110 PCF, from EL-0 to EL-3, with the water table at EL-3; soft organic clay, γb = 40 PCF, from EL-3 to EL-15; firm sand, φ = 30°, γb = 65 PCF, below EL-15. The piles are battered at 1 horizontal to 2 vertical, with their toes at EL-33; the pile cap is 10' × 11' in plan. FOR A SIX PILE GROUP - 4 TENSION, 2 COMPRESSION ASSUME A 14" SQUARE STRAIGHT CONCRETE PILE, AS SHOWN, D = 20' (D < 20B). PILE CAP WEIGHT (DW) = 10 X 11 X 3 X 0.15 KCF = 49.5 K. FIND Fs AGAINST Qult AND Tult. DETERMINE PILE FORCES BY A FORCE DIAGRAM. IGNORE RESISTANCE ABOVE FIRM SAND STRATUM. Values read in the example: from the force diagram (scale 1" = 40 K) the compression load on the piles is 70 kips, carried by the 2 compression piles, and the tension load is 80 kips, carried by the 4 tension piles; for the bearing stratum Nq = 21, KHC = 1.5, KHT = 1.0 and δ = 3/4 φ (Figure 1). Qult = σ'v,toe Nq AT + KHC σ'v,avg tan δ × (perimeter) × D and Tult = KHT σ'v,avg tan δ × (perimeter) × D, where σ'v,avg is the mean of the vertical effective stresses at the top (EL-15) and toe (EL-33) of the bearing stratum, AT is the pile toe area and D = 20 ft. Fs against Qult = Qult/(compression load per pile); Fs against Tult = Tult/(tension load per pile − weight of pile), the weight of pile taken at 0.15 KCF over a 37 ft pile length. Determine the vertical effective stress at the top (EL-15) and at the toe level (EL-33) of the bearing stratum, in ksf.

statement: A 1.5-ft diameter straight concrete drilled shaft is to be constructed 30 ft deep through a 2-layer soil of a slightly overconsolidated clay with PI = 40 and fine uniform sand, Figure 5-7. Depth of embedment in the sand layer Lb = 15 ft. The water table is 15 ft below ground surface at the clay-sand interface. The concrete unit weight γconc = 150 lbs/ft3. Design load Qd = 75 kips. Figure 5-7 (Drilled shaft 1.5-ft diameter at 30-ft depth): clay from the ground surface, Lclay = 15 ft, γc = 0.12 kip/ft3, Cu = 2 ksf; sand below, Lsand = 15 ft, γs = 0.10 kip/ft3, γ's = 0.04 kip/ft3, φ' = 36°, c = 0; the water table is at the clay-sand interface. Laboratory strength tests indicate that the average undrained shear strength of the clay is Cu = 2 ksf. Cone penetration tests indicate an average cone tip resistance qc in the clay is 40 ksf and in the sand 160 ksf. Effective stresses: σ's denotes the mean effective vertical stress in the sand layer adjacent to the shaft (Eq. 5-13a) and σ'L the effective vertical stress at the shaft tip (Eq. 5-13b); the end bearing methods below use σ'L. Relative density of the sand at the shaft tip by Eq. 3-5: Dr (percent) = -74 + 66·log10[qc/√(σ'vo)], with qc and σ'vo in ksf and σ'vo the effective vertical stress at the shaft tip. Hansen method for end bearing (Eq. 5-2a): qbu = σ'L·Nqp·ζqp + (Bb/2)·γ'b·Nγp·ζγp, with Bb = 1.5 ft and γ'b = 0.04 kip/ft3; Hansen factors Nqp = e^(π·tanφ')·tan²(45 + φ'/2) and Nγp = 1.5·(Nqp - 1)·tanφ' (Table 4-4); ζqp = ζqs·ζqd with ζqs = 1 + tanφ' and ζqd = 1 + 2·tanφ'·(1 - sinφ')²·tan⁻¹(Lsand/B), the arctangent taken in radians; ζγp = ζγs·ζγd = 0.6·1.00 (Table 4-5). Vesic method: qbu = σ'L·Nqp·ζqp (Eq. 5-2c), with Nqp = [3/(3 - sinφ')]·exp[(90 - φ')·(π/180)·tanφ']·tan²(45 + φ'/2)·Irr^[4·sinφ'/(3·(1 + sinφ'))] (Eq. 5-5b); reduced rigidity index Irr = Ir/(1 + εv·Ir) (Eq. 5-5c), with εv = [(1 - 2νs)/(2·(1 - νs))]·σ'L/Gs (Eq. 5-5e) and Ir = Gs/(c + σ'L·tanφ') (Eq. 5-5d); shape factor ζqp = (1 + 2Ko)/3 (Eq. 5-6a) with Ko = 1 - sinφ' (Jaky Equation 5-6c). Take the sand shear modulus Gs = 100 ksf and Poisson's ratio νs = 0.3. General shear method: Nqp = exp[((270 - φ')/180)·π·tanφ'] / [2·cos²(45 + φ'/2)] (Eq. 5-8), shape factor ζqp = 1.00, and qbu = σ'L·Nqp·ζqp (Eq. 5-2c). Skin friction in the clay by Eq. 5-10, fs = αa·Cu, with αa = 0.9 - 0.01·PI (Eq. 5-11b). Skin friction in the sand by Eq. 5-12a, fs = βf·σ's, where the effective stress is limited by Lc/B = 10 to depth Lc = 15 ft measured from the ground surface: for skin friction use the effective vertical stress at 15 ft below the ground surface (the clay-sand interface) in place of the Eq. 5-13a mean; βf = 0.26 from Figure 5-5 (drilled shafts, φ' = 36 deg). Total capacity Qu = Qbu + Qsu - Wp (Eq. 5-1a), with Qbu = qbu·Ab, Ab = πB²/4 (Eq. 5-1b), and Qsu = πB·ΣL·fs (Eqs. 5-1b and 5-9), skin friction ignored in the top 5 ft of clay. Shaft weight Wp = (πB²/4)·(Lclay·γconc + Lsand·γ'conc), with γ'conc = 86 lbs/ft3 below the water table. Allowable capacity Qa = Qu/FS with FS = 3 (Table 1-2). Determine the mean effective vertical stress σ's in the sand layer adjacent to the shaft and the effective vertical stress σ'L at the shaft tip, in ksf.

Figure 5-7 (Drilled shaft 1.5-ft diameter at 30-ft depth): clay from the ground surface, Lclay = 15 ft, γc = 0.12 kip/ft3, Cu = 2 ksf; sand below, Lsand = 15 ft, γs = 0.10 kip/ft3, γ's = 0.04 kip/ft3, φ' = 36°, c = 0; the water table is at the clay-sand interface. Laboratory strength tests indicate that the average undrained shear strength of the clay is Cu = 2 ksf. Cone penetration tests indicate an average cone tip resistance qc in the clay is 40 ksf and in the sand 160 ksf. Effective stresses: σ's denotes the mean effective vertical stress in the sand layer adjacent to the shaft (Eq. 5-13a) and σ'L the effective vertical stress at the shaft tip (Eq. 5-13b); the end bearing methods below use σ'L. Relative density of the sand at the shaft tip by Eq. 3-5: Dr (percent) = -74 + 66·log10[qc/√(σ'vo)], with qc and σ'vo in ksf and σ'vo the effective vertical stress at the shaft tip. Hansen method for end bearing (Eq. 5-2a): qbu = σ'L·Nqp·ζqp + (Bb/2)·γ'b·Nγp·ζγp, with Bb = 1.5 ft and γ'b = 0.04 kip/ft3; Hansen factors Nqp = e^(π·tanφ')·tan²(45 + φ'/2) and Nγp = 1.5·(Nqp - 1)·tanφ' (Table 4-4); ζqp = ζqs·ζqd with ζqs = 1 + tanφ' and ζqd = 1 + 2·tanφ'·(1 - sinφ')²·tan⁻¹(Lsand/B), the arctangent taken in radians; ζγp = ζγs·ζγd = 0.6·1.00 (Table 4-5). Vesic method: qbu = σ'L·Nqp·ζqp (Eq. 5-2c), with Nqp = [3/(3 - sinφ')]·exp[(90 - φ')·(π/180)·tanφ']·tan²(45 + φ'/2)·Irr^[4·sinφ'/(3·(1 + sinφ'))] (Eq. 5-5b); reduced rigidity index Irr = Ir/(1 + εv·Ir) (Eq. 5-5c), with εv = [(1 - 2νs)/(2·(1 - νs))]·σ'L/Gs (Eq. 5-5e) and Ir = Gs/(c + σ'L·tanφ') (Eq. 5-5d); shape factor ζqp = (1 + 2Ko)/3 (Eq. 5-6a) with Ko = 1 - sinφ' (Jaky Equation 5-6c). Take the sand shear modulus Gs = 100 ksf and Poisson's ratio νs = 0.3. General shear method: Nqp = exp[((270 - φ')/180)·π·tanφ'] / [2·cos²(45 + φ'/2)] (Eq. 5-8), shape factor ζqp = 1.00, and qbu = σ'L·Nqp·ζqp (Eq. 5-2c). Skin friction in the clay by Eq. 5-10, fs = αa·Cu, with αa = 0.9 - 0.01·PI (Eq. 5-11b). Skin friction in the sand by Eq. 5-12a, fs = βf·σ's, where the effective stress is limited by Lc/B = 10 to depth Lc = 15 ft measured from the ground surface: for skin friction use the effective vertical stress at 15 ft below the ground surface (the clay-sand interface) in place of the Eq. 5-13a mean; βf = 0.26 from Figure 5-5 (drilled shafts, φ' = 36 deg). Total capacity Qu = Qbu + Qsu - Wp (Eq. 5-1a), with Qbu = qbu·Ab, Ab = πB²/4 (Eq. 5-1b), and Qsu = πB·ΣL·fs (Eqs. 5-1b and 5-9), skin friction ignored in the top 5 ft of clay. Shaft weight Wp = (πB²/4)·(Lclay·γconc + Lsand·γ'conc), with γ'conc = 86 lbs/ft3 below the water table. Allowable capacity Qa = Qu/FS with FS = 3 (Table 1-2). Using the manual's selected end bearing capacity qbu = 102 ksf and selected skin friction of 1 ksf in the clay and 1 ksf in the sand, determine the shaft weight Wp, the end bearing capacity Qbu, the skin resistance Qsu and the total ultimate capacity Qu, in kips.

statement: A steel circular 1.5-ft diameter closed end pipe pile is to be driven 30 ft through a 2-layer soil of clay and fine uniform sand, Figure 5-7. The water table is 15 ft below ground surface at the clay-sand interface. The pile will be filled with concrete grout with density γconc = 150 lbs/ft3. Design load Qd = 100 kips. Figure 5-7 (soil profile): clay from the ground surface, Lclay = 15 ft, γc = 0.12 kip/ft3, Cu = 2 ksf; sand below, Lsand = 15 ft, γs = 0.10 kip/ft3, γ's = 0.04 kip/ft3, φ' = 36°, c = 0; the water table is at the clay-sand interface. The average undrained shear strength of the upper clay layer is Cu = 2 ksf. The friction angle of the lower sand layer is estimated at φ' = 36 deg. Cone penetration test results indicate an average cone tip resistance qc = 40 ksf in the clay and 160 ksf in the sand. Critical depth: from Figure 5-3, Rc = 10 for φ' = 36 deg, so Lc = Rc·B = 15 ft, measured from the ground surface. For the Meyerhof and Nordlund methods and for the sand skin friction (Eq. 5-12a and Table 5-8b), the effective vertical stress adjacent to the pile in the sand (σ's, σ'z) and at the pile tip (σ'L) is the limiting stress: the effective vertical stress at 15 ft below the ground surface (the clay-sand interface). Meyerhof method: qbu = σ'L·Nqp (Eq. 5-2c), not more than the limiting pressure ql = Nqp·tanφ' in ksf (Eq. 5-31c as applied), with Nqp = 170 from Figure 5-15 for Rb = L/B = 15/1.5 = 10. Nordlund method for end bearing (Table 5-8a): qbu = αf·Nqp·σ'L, not more than ql = Nqp·tanφ' ksf with Nqp = 170 from Figure 5-15; αf = 0.67 (Figure 5-17a) and Nqp = 80 (Figure 5-17b) for φ' = 36 deg. CPT Meyerhof method (Eq. 5-34): qbu = (qc/10)·(Lsand/B), not more than ql = Nqp·tanφ' ksf (Nqp = 170, Figure 5-15). CPT B & G method (Eq. 5-35): qbu = kc·qc with kc = 0.375 for a driven pile in sand-gravel (Table 5-9). Skin friction in the clay: Alpha method fs = αa·Cu (Eq. 5-10) with αa = 1.2 - 0.3·Cu (Cu in ksf, L/B < 20); Lambda method fs = λ·(σ'm + 2Cum) (Eq. 5-38a) with λ = L^-0.42 (Eq. 5-38b), L = 15 ft for the penetration of the pile only in the clay, σ'm = (Dc/2)·γ'clay with Dc = 15 ft and γ'clay = 0.12 kip/ft3, and Cum = 2 ksf. Skin friction in the sand: Eq. 5-12a, fs = βf·σ's, σ's the limiting stress, with βf = 0.96 from Figure 5-5 (driven piles, φ' = 36 deg). Nordlund method of Table 5-8b: Qsz = K·Cf·σ'z·sinδ·Cz·z over the sand thickness z = 15 ft, with K = 2.1 (Figure 5-18, ω = 0 deg), δ = 0.78·φ' (Figure 5-19, V = 1.77 ft3/ft, pile type 1), Cf = 0.91 (Figure 5-20), σ'z the limiting stress, and Cz = π·B with B = 1.5 ft; then fs = Qsz/(Cz·z). Ultimate total capacity Qu = Qbu + Qsu - Wp (Eq. 5-1a), with Qbu = Ab·qbu, Ab = πB²/4 (Eq. 5-1b); Qsu = πB·(Lsand·fs + Lclay·fs) (Eqs. 5-1b and 5-9) over the full clay and sand thicknesses; pile weight Wp = (πB²/4)·L·γconc with L = 30 ft. By the Meyerhof method, determine the end bearing capacity qbu of the pile tip in the sand, in ksf.

statement: Example 2. This example will illustrate the method of fragment procedure for unconfined flow problems. The example is obtained from John H. Overton Lock and Dam (U. S. Army Engineer District, St. Louis 1978). The problem is to locate the free surface in the closure dam and to determine the quantity of flow through the dam under steady state conditions. The dimensions of the structure shown in figure B-17 are after the material has been transformed to account for soil anisotropy. This sample problem assumes an impervious boundary at the base of the dam. To account for some flow under the dam, the impervious boundary could be lowered. By lowering the boundary to the lowest possible point, bounds for the problem would be established. There are three fragment types in this earthen embankment. Region 1 is a type VIII fragment while region 2 is a type VII fragment and region 3 is a type IX fragment. Figure B-17 (transformed section of John H. Overton closure dam): impervious base at EL. 26; crest at EL. 63 with crest width b = 133 FT; upstream water surface EL. 58, h1 (32 FT); h0 (37 FT) from the base to the crest; upstream slope angle α = 19.9°; downstream slope angle β = 26.5°; tailwater EL. 40, h2 (14 FT); K = 500 x 10^-4 CM/SEC = 141.7 FT/DAY. In the figure, h is the height of the free surface above the base at the upstream end of region 2 (the vertical through the upstream crest edge), a2 is the height of the seepage exit point on the downstream slope above the tailwater, and L is the length of region 2 between the upstream crest edge and the vertical through the exit point. Use the method of fragments with continuity of flow Q through the three regions. Region 1 (type VIII fragment, Eq. B-18): Q = k (h1 - h)/cot α · ln[hd/(hd - h)] with h1 = 32 ft, hd = 37 ft and cot α = 2.76. Region 2 (type VII fragment, Eq. B-15 with the upstream and downstream heads h and a2 + h2): Q = k [h^2 - (a2 + h2)^2]/(2L). Region 3 (type IX fragment, Eq. B-19): Q = k a2/cot β · [1 + ln((a2 + h2)/a2)] with cot β = 2 and h2 = 14 ft. From the embankment geometry (Eq. B-26), L = b + cot β [hd - (a2 + h2)] with b = 133 ft. ln is the natural logarithm. Solve the equations simultaneously for h, a2, Q/k and L; the flow uses k = 141.7 ft/day. Determine the height h of the free surface at the upstream end of region 2, in ft.

statement: Figure 4-10. Example of technique for developing a flow net for an anisotropic foundation. (a) True cross section of dam: an impervious dam (k → 0) with a 20-ft crest, upstream and downstream slopes of 2½:1 and a base 220 ft wide rests on an anisotropic foundation, kh = 100 kv, 40 ft thick over an impervious boundary. The net head across the dam is h = 36 ft (reservoir level above the tailwater level at the ground surface). (b) A flow net is drawn on the transformed section and (c) transposed to the true scale to obtain the seepage quantity and the exit gradient at the downstream toe. Draw the flow net on a transformed section whose horizontal dimensions are multiplied by the horizontal transformation factor √(kv/kh) (the dam base becomes 22 ft wide; the 40-ft depth is unchanged). Use the transformed permeability k' = √(kv·kh), and the seepage per unit length of dam q = k' h (Nf/Nd). The squared flow net on the transformed section (Figure 4-10(b)) has Nf = 6.65 flow channels (six full channels and a 0.65 flow channel) and Nd = 10 equipotential drops. In the toe area of the flow net transposed to true scale (Figure 4-10(c), toe area enlarged), the last equipotential drop occupies a length ΔL = 3.0 ft along the exit face; the exit gradient is ie = Δh/ΔL with Δh the head lost in one drop. Determine the seepage quantity per unit length of dam expressed as q/k', in ft (q = (q/k')·k').

statement: A composite embankment section (Figure 6-15) has zone 1 with permeability k1 and zone 2 with permeability k2; the section was assumed to have k2 = 5k1. The head h between the reservoir level and the tailwater level is divided into equal increments Δh, and a trial flow net is drawn with squares in zone 1 and rectangles in zone 2. To check the trial flow net, count the number of full flow channels between any two adjacent equipotential lines in zone 1 (nf-1) and in zone 2 (nf-2). In the first trial flow net (figure 6-15a), nf-1 = 4.0, and nf-2, equal to the width-to-length ratio d/c of the figures in zone 2, is 0.5. In the second trial flow net (figure 6-15b), nf-1 = 3.5 and nf-2 = 0.7. Calculate the actual ratio of k2/k1 for each trial flow net. The actual permeability ratio of a trial composite flow net follows from equal seepage in both zones, q = k1 h (nf-1/nd) = k2 h (nf-2/nd), so k2/k1 = nf-1/nf-2. Determine the actual ratio k2/k1 for the first trial flow net (figure 6-15a) (dimensionless).

statement: Example: Determine the quantity of seepage, q, a0, and h1, using Pavlovsky's solution for the dam shown above. Compare with Schaffernak-Van Iterson and L. Casagrande Method, figure 6-2. For this case: cot α = cot β = 3 b = 20' hd = 80' hw = 70' h0 = 0 k = 0.002 ft/min. The dam shown (Figure 6-8) is a homogeneous embankment on an impervious foundation: reservoir depth 70 ft, freeboard 10 ft to the crest, crest width 20 ft, upstream and downstream slopes 1 vertical on 3 horizontal, no tailwater. A. Pavlovsky's solution (h0 = 0): a0 and h1 are the intersection of Eq. 6-5, a0 = (cot α/cot β)(hw - h1) ln[hd/(hd - h1)], and Eq. 6-6, a0 = b/cot α + hd - √[(b/cot α + hd)^2 - h1^2]; then q = k a0/cot α (Eq. 6-4). ln is the natural logarithm; a0 is the height of the seepage exit point on the downstream slope and h1 the height of the line of seepage at the upstream crest edge. B. Schaffernak-Van Iterson (Figure 6-2, α < 30°): a = d/cos α - √(d^2/cos^2 α - h^2/sin^2 α) and q = k a sin α tan α, where α is the downstream slope angle (cot α = 3, α = 18°26'), h = hw = 70 ft, and d is the horizontal distance from the point 0.3m upstream of the intersection of the reservoir surface with the upstream slope to the downstream toe, m being the horizontal projection of the wetted upstream slope. C. L. Casagrande (Figure 6-2): a = s0 - √(s0^2 - h^2/sin^2 α) with s0 = √(d^2 + h^2) (α ≤ 60°) and q = k a sin^2 α. Determine a0 by Pavlovsky's solution, in ft.

statement: Figure 8-9 shows an example of the design procedure for inclined and horizontal drains to assure adequate drain capacity (Cedergren 1977). The probable rate of discharge through the dam and foundation is estimated from composite flow nets (see figures 4-13 and 4-14). For the example shown in figure 8-9, the seepage through the dam Q1 = 2 cu ft/day and the seepage through the foundation Q2 = 10 cu ft/day. Therefore, the inclined drain must be capable of discharging Q1 = 2 cu ft/day and the horizontal drain must be capable to discharging Q1 + Q2 = 12 cu ft/day. These are discharge rates per running foot of dam and drain. Assuming the inclined drain was designed with a width of 12 ft to permit its placement with normal earth-moving equipment, the cross-sectional area normal to the direction of flow within the inclined drain Ac = 11 sq ft (see figure 8-9b) and its required minimum permeability may be found from Darcy's law. Figure 8-9: (a) dam with h = 300 ft, rolled impervious core k = 0.01 ft/day, "chimney" drain and blanket drain on a fractured rock foundation; (b) inclined drain: Tc = 12 ft, hc = 300 ft, Lc = 310 ft, Qc = Q1; (c) horizontal drain: hb = Ab, Lb = 550 ft, Qb = Q1 + Q2. Darcy's law k = Q/(iA) (Eq. 8-2). For the inclined drain i = hc/Lc and A = Ac. Every filter must have a minimum permeability after placement and compaction of at least 20 times that calculated theoretically (kdesign = 20k). For the horizontal drain the allowable maximum head can be no greater than its height, so i = hb/Lb and Ab = hb (width is one running foot of dam and drain); select a drain height hb = 4 ft. Determine the theoretical minimum permeability kc of the inclined drain, in ft/day.

statement: Figure 9-1. Influence of horizontal drain on uplift pressure. An impervious dam with net head h rests on a pervious foundation over an impervious base, the tailwater at the ground surface downstream; c and d mark the upstream and downstream ends of the base. The flow net is drawn without a drain (W/O DRAIN) and with a drainage blanket under the downstream part of the dam (W/DRAIN). The shape factor is the ratio of number of flow channels to number of flow paths in the flow net. The flow net without a drain has 2 flow channels and 7 equipotential drops; the flow net with the drainage blanket has 2 flow channels and 5 equipotential drops. Shape factor = number of flow channels / number of drops. Determine the shape factor of the flow net without a drain (dimensionless).

statement: Figure E-13 shows a slope where a relatively thin layer of soil overlies firm soil. The critical failure mechanism for this example is sliding along a plane parallel to the slope, at the top of the firm layer. This slope can be analyzed using the infinite slope stability chart shown in Figure E-7. Calculate the factor of safety for seepage parallel to the slope and for horizontal seepage emerging from the slope. Figure E-13 (example of an infinite slope analysis): γ = 120 pcf, c′ = 300 psf, φ′ = 30°, tan φ′ = 0.577; β = 20°, tan β = 0.364, cot β = 2.75. The soil layer above the firm layer is 12 ft deep measured vertically and 11.3 ft thick measured perpendicular to the slope; the surface of seepage, parallel to the slope, lies 8 ft above the top of the firm layer measured perpendicular to the slope. Use the infinite slope charts of Figure E-7 (after Duncan, Buchianani, and DeWet 1987): for seepage parallel to the slope r_u = (X/T)(γw/γ) cos²β with X = 8 ft and T = 11.3 ft; for seepage emerging from the slope r_u = (γw/γ)/(1 + tan β tan θ), with θ = 0° for horizontal seepage; factor of safety F = A tan φ′/tan β + B c′/(γH) with H = 12 ft, the depth measured vertically; γw = 62.4 pcf; cos β taken as 0.94. Chart readings of the example from Figure E-7 with cot β = 2.75: A = 0.62 and B = 3.1 for the r_u of seepage parallel to the slope; A = 0.41 and B = 3.1 for the r_u of horizontal seepage. Determine the pore pressure ratio r_u for seepage parallel to the slope (dimensionless).

statement: Example calculations are presented for stability at the end of construction of the embankment shown in Figure F-10. The embankment cross section contains two materials -- the embankment soil and the foundation soil. Both soils are fine-grained and undrained during construction. For the example problem illustrated in Figure F-10, all water pressures are zero, because there is no external water. Total unit weights are used for all soils. Figure F-10: the slope rises from the toe at EL. 0 on a 3:1 slope to EL. 58 ft and then on a 2.5:1 slope to the crest at EL. 91 ft. The center of the circle is 101 ft horizontally from the toe and 259 ft above it; R = 278 ft. Material properties: embankment, total unit weight γ = 135 pcf, c = 1780 psf, φ = 5°; foundation, γ = 127 pcf, c = 1600 psf, φ = 2°. The soil above the circle is divided into ten slices numbered 1 (at the crest) to 10 (at the toe). Slice data of the example (Figure F-11c, all slices): slice: horizontal width b (ft), total weight W (kips), base inclination α (degrees), base length Δℓ (ft), c (ksf), φ (degrees). 1: 17, 30, 48, 25.8, 1.78, 5. 2: 22, 108, 43, 29.9, 1.78, 5. 3: 22, 158, 37, 26.8, 1.78, 5. 4: 29, 251, 31, 33.1, 1.78, 5. 5: 26, 241, 24, 28.5, 1.78, 5. 6: 28, 257, 18, 29.5, 1.60, 2. 7: 37, 320, 11, 37.7, 1.60, 2. 8: 36, 275, 4, 36.1, 1.60, 2. 9: 44, 253, −5, 44.1, 1.60, 2. 10: 57, 129, −15, 59.1, 1.60, 2. The bottoms of slices 1 through 5 are in the embankment and slices 6 through 10 in the foundation; slices are numbered from the crest toward the toe. Use the Simplified Bishop Method: F = Σ[(cΔx + W tan φ)/mα] / Σ W sin α with Δx = b and mα = cos α + sin α tan φ / F, iterated until the assumed and computed F agree; slice strengths are those of the soil at the bottom of the slice. Use the Modified Swedish Method, numerical solution, with the interslice force inclination equal to the average embankment slope, 2.8 (horizontal) to 1 (vertical): θ = arctan(1/2.8) = 19.7 degrees. For a trial F, set Z1 = 0 for the first slice and compute the interslice force on the downslope side of each slice by Equation F-7, Z(i+1) = Zi + {W[sin α − tan φ cos α / F] − c Δℓ / F} / [cos(α − θ) + tan φ sin(α − θ)/F]; a negative interslice force is set to zero for the next slice. The force on the downslope side of the last slice is the force imbalance; the factor of safety is the trial F that makes it zero. For the Simplified Bishop Method, determine the sum Σ W sin α over all slices, in kips.

statement: Figure F-15 shows an embankment with steady seepage. The cross section contains two principal zones -- the embankment fill and the foundation. There are also three smaller zones of material in the embankment: an upstream layer of rip-rap, an internal chimney drain and a horizontal drainage blanket. For these example stability calculations, all of these smaller zones were treated as being the same as the embankment. The trial slip surface used for the computations does not intersect any of the smaller zones, and their strength properties therefore do not influence the results of the analyses. Figure F-15: embankment, total unit weight γ = 130 lbs./cu.ft., c′ = 0, φ′ = 34°; foundation, γ = 125 lbs./cu.ft., c′ = 0, φ′ = 35°. Crest at El. 112, reservoir at El. 99.5, downstream slope through El. 73.5 to the toe at El. 0, tailwater at El. 22.5, foundation from El. 0 to El. -32. Figure F-16: circular slip surface of radius R = 280 ft with its centre 131 ft horizontally and 248 ft vertically from the downstream toe, divided into nine slices; there is water on the external surface of the slope above the last slice, Slice 9. statement: Find the lateral forces and pressures acting on the wall for the seismic condition. Soil properties (on both sides of wall): γ = 0.12 k/ft3 (moist weight), γb = 0.0625 k/ft3 (buoyancy weight), γs = 0.125 k/ft3 (saturated weight), φ = 35°, c = 0. Seismic coefficients: kH = 0.20, kv = 0. Figure: concrete gravity wall, γ (CONCRETE) = 0.15 KCF, base 18' wide, height 25' = h with a vertical back face on the driving side, crest 6' wide; the front face slopes from the crest down to a point 6' above the base at the toe (12' horizontally), then is vertical to the base. Driving side: the backfill surface rises from the top of the wall at 3 horizontal to 1 vertical (angle β); water table 12' = hs above the base. Resisting side: level ground (β = 0) 6' = hs above the base, with the water table at the ground surface. Uplift under the base varies linearly from 0.75 KSF at the heel to 0.375 KSF at the toe. Driving side, seismic active wedge with the full φ (no strength mobilization factor): c1 = 2(tan φ − kh)/(1 + kh tan φ) (Eq. 3-57), c2 = [tan φ (1 − tan φ tan β) − (tan β + kh)]/[tan φ (1 + kh tan φ)] (Eq. 3-58), α = tan⁻¹[(c1 + √(c1² + 4c2))/2] (Eq. 3-56); K = (1 − tan φ cot α)/(1 + tan φ tan α), KA = K tan α/(tan α − tan β) (Eq. 3-54), Kb = K[1 + (tan α/(tan α − tan β) − 1)(γ/γb)] (Appendix H); static force PA = ½KAγ(h − hs)² + ½hs[2KAγ(h − hs) + Kbγbhs] (Eq. 3-69), pressure KAγ times the depth down to the water table then increasing by Kbγb per foot; dynamic increment ΔPAE = kh[γh²/(2(tan α − tan β)) + (γs − γ)hs²/(2 tan α)] (Eq. 3-71); water force Pws = ½γw hs² (Eq. 3-70), with γw = γs − γb. Each part of ΔPAE is distributed as an inverted triangle (maximum at its top, zero at the base): the moist-weight part kh γh²/[2(tan α − tan β)] over the full height h, the (γs − γ) part over hs. Permissible simplification: take the soil weight above and below the water table equal to the moist weight (moist-weight part only). Resisting side (Mononobe-Okabe passive wedge, full φ): c1 = 2(tan φ − kh)/(1 + kh tan φ) (Eq. 3-60), c2 = (tan φ − kh)/[tan φ (1 + kh tan φ)] (Eq. 3-61), α = tan⁻¹[(−c1 + √(c1² + 4c2))/2] (Eq. 3-59); KP = (1 + tan φ cot α)/(1 − tan φ tan α) (Eq. 3-77); PP = ½KPγbh² over h = 6 ft (Eq. 3-73); ΔPPE = kh γs h²/(2 tan α) (Eq. 3-75); Pws = ½γw hs² (Eq. 3-74). Inertia force due to the weight of the wall: kh W, acting at the height of the centroid of the wall section above the base. Determine the critical slip-plane angle α on the driving side, in degrees.
