statement: Find lateral soil force (PEE) that will act on Surface ABC. Show the effect of water on slip-plane angle (α), and earth force. Figure: the backfill surface slopes up away from the wall at 4 horizontal to 1 vertical (angle β) and meets the vertical plane ABC at A; ABC is the vertical plane through the heel C of the wall base, h = 20.25'. The water table is at B, 2.25' + 2' below A, with hs = 16' from B down to C. A strip surcharge V = 6 K/FT acts on the backfill surface, spread uniformly between 2' and 6' horizontally from A (dimensions 2', 2', 2' measured from A). The driving wedge lies between ABC and the slip plane rising from C at angle α; its top width is h/(tan α − tan β). A line from C through the far edge of the surcharge is marked at 74.5778° to the horizontal. Stem 9' from A. γM = 0.120 KCF, γS = 0.125 KCF, γB = 0.0625 KCF, Φ = 35°, c = 0, SMF = 2/3, Φd = 25°. Slip-plane angle neglecting the effect of water: Eqs. 3-28 to 3-30 with the c terms omitted: A = tan φd − 2V(1 + tan² φd)/(γh²) (Eq. 3-30), c1 = [2 tan² φd − 4V tan β (1 + tan² φd)/(γh²)]/A (Eq. 3-28), c2 = [tan φd (1 − tan φd tan β) − tan β + 2V tan² β (1 + tan² φd)/(γh²)]/A (Eq. 3-29), and α = tan⁻¹[(c1 + √(c1² + 4c2))/2] (Eq. 3-25), with γ = γm. To include the effect of water, use in the same equations, in place of γm, the average unit weight γavg = [γm h²/(2(tan α − tan β)) − (γm − γb) hs²/(2 tan α)] ÷ [h²/(2(tan α − tan β))], evaluated at α = 74.5778°, with γavg rounded to three decimal places (kcf) before use. If the resulting angle exceeds 74.5778°, use α = 74.5778°: at a steeper angle the entire surcharge does not lie on the top surface of the wedge. Coefficients (Appendix H): K = (1 − tan φd cot α)/(1 + tan φd tan α), K1 = K tan α/(tan α − tan β), Kb = K[1 + (tan α/(tan α − tan β) − 1)(γm/γb)], Kv = K tan α. Forces: Pγ = ½K1γm(h − hs)² + ½hs[2K1γm(h − hs) + Kbγbhs], PV = KvV, PEE = Pγ + PV. The Pγ pressure is K1γm times the depth below A down to the water table, then increases by Kbγb per foot below it. Iteration of Eq. 3-23 (simplified): PEE = [(W + V)(tan α − tan φd) + U tan φd/cos α]/(1 + tan φd tan α) − Pw, with W = γm h²/[2(tan α − tan β)] + (γs − γm) hs²/(2 tan α), U = γw hs²/(2 sin α), Pw = γw hs²/2 and γw = 0.0625 kcf; when the slip plane meets the surface inside the loaded strip, only the part of V lying on the wedge (in proportion to the loaded width on the wedge) is included. The maximum PEE governs. Line of action of PV by the approximate method of Figure 3-29: from the point of application of V (its resultant, 4' horizontally from A, on the backfill surface) draw two lines downward toward the plane ABC, inclined to the horizontal at φ = 35° (the full friction angle, not φd) and at α', where α' is the slip-plane angle without surcharge from Eqs. 3-26 and 3-27 with SMF = 1.00 (c1 = 2 tan φ, c2 = 1 − tan φ tan β − tan β/tan φ, Eq. 3-25). PV acts at one third of the distance between the two intersection points, measured from the upper one. For the pressure diagram, the pressure due to V is an isosceles triangle with its apex at the point of application of PV and its upper end at A. The horizontal earth pressure at C is the effective soil pressure only (the Pγ diagram plus the PV triangle), excluding water pressure. Neglecting the effect of water, determine the slip-plane angle α, in degrees.

statement: Find lateral earth force acting on Surface ABC. Use moist unit weight of soil to calculate α. Check solution by iteration of Equation 3-23. Figure: the backfill surface slopes up away from the wall at 4 horizontal to 1 vertical (angle β) and meets the vertical back face ABC of the wall at A; h = 18' from A down to C, the water table at B with hs = 10' from B down to C. The driving wedge is bounded by a tension crack of depth dc at its upper end and by the slip plane rising from C at angle α. γMOIST = 0.120 KCF, γSAT. = 0.125 KCF, γBOUY. = 0.0625 KCF, Φ = 0, c = 0.60 KCF, SMF = 2/3, cd = 0.40 KSF, tan β = 1/4. Slip-plane angle with the moist unit weight γm (Eqs. 3-28 to 3-30 with φ = 0): A = 2cd/[γm(h + dc)], c1 = [4cd tan β/(γm(h + dc))]/A, c2 = [−tan β + 2cd/(γm(h + dc))]/A, α = tan⁻¹[(c1 + √(c1² + 4c2))/2] (Eq. 3-25), with the tension-crack depth dc = (cd/γm)/(sin α cos α) (Equation I-2 with φ = 0, Appendix I). Start from an estimate α = 40° and repeat until α converges; take α to the nearest degree and compute dc at that angle. Coefficients (Appendix H): K = (1 − tan φd cot α)/(1 + tan φd tan α), K1 = K tan α/(tan α − tan β), Kb = K[1 + (tan α/(tan α − tan β) − 1)(γm/γb)]. statement: Find the lateral earth forces on Surfaces CD and DE (stratified soil). Figure: the wall face CDE is vertical, C at the top of the backfill against the wall, D at the boundary between the two soils, E at the base of the wall; h1 = 13' from C to D, h2 = 10' from D to E, 23' in all. The ground surface rises from C away from the wall at 3 horizontal to 1 vertical (angle β1). The boundary between soil 1 (above) and soil 2 (below) rises from D away from the wall at 6 horizontal to 1 vertical (angle β2). Wedge 2, in soil 2, lies between DE and the slip plane rising from E at angle α2 to point B on the soil boundary; wedge 1, in soil 1, lies between the vertical plane AB and the slip plane rising from B at angle α1 to the ground surface. A is on the ground surface above B; the horizontal distance from AB to the wall is 10/(tan α2 − tan β2); Z is on the vertical through C at the level of A (triangle ACZ). Soil 1: γ1 = 0.12 KCF, Φ1 = 35°, SMF = 2/3, Φd1 = 25°. Soil 2: γ2 = 0.13 KCF, Φ2 = 20°, SMF = 2/3, Φd2 = 13.64°. Slip-plane angle α2 by Eqs. G-25 to G-30 (Appendix G): γ' = 2γ1h1/h2 + γ2 + 2γ1(tan β1 − tan β2)/(tan α2 − tan β2) (G-25); the weight of the surcharge in triangle ACZ Vα = −γ1h2²(tan β1 − tan β2)/[2(tan α2 − tan β2)²] (G-26); A' = tan φd2 − 2Vα(1 + tan² φd2)/(γ'h2²) (G-27); c'1 = [2 tan² φd2 − 4Vα tan β2 (1 + tan² φd2)/(γ'h2²)]/A' (G-28); c'2 = [tan φd2 (1 − tan φd2 tan β2) − tan β2 + 2Vα tan² β2 (1 + tan² φd2)/(γ'h2²)]/A' (G-29); α2 = tan⁻¹[(c'1 + √(c'1² + 4c'2))/2] (G-30). Start from a first trial α2 = 39° and repeat until the trial and computed angles agree; take α2 to the nearest degree and use the rounded α2 in all later steps. Slip-plane angle α1 by Eqs. 3-26 and 3-27 with φd1 and β1: c1 = 2 tan φd1, c2 = 1 − tan φd1 tan β1 − tan β1/tan φd1, α1 = tan⁻¹[(c1 + √(c1² + 4c2))/2]. Coefficients (Appendix H) for each wedge with its own φd, α and β: K = (1 − tan φd cot α)/(1 + tan φd tan α), K1 = K tan α/(tan α − tan β); for wedge 2 also Kv = K tan α. Wedge 1: hAB = h1 + h2(tan β1 − tan β2)/(tan α2 − tan β2); PEE1 = ½K1γ1hAB² on AB, with horizontal pressure pHB = K1γ1hAB at B. Wedge 2: treat the weight of ABCD as a strip surcharge on Surface BD, V = ½(h1 + hAB)(AZ)(γ1) with AZ = h2/(tan α2 − tan β2); Pγ = ½K1γ2h2², PV = KvV, PEE2 = Pγ + PV; the horizontal pressure at D is pHD = K1 (wedge 2) times γ1h1 and at E pHE = 2PEE2/h2 − pHD, linear between D and E. The earth force on AB is transferred to Surface CD by assuming that no shear resistance is developed on Surface BD; moment equilibrium of Block ABCD (about D) then requires equal and opposite vertical shear forces VAB on AB and VCD on CD. PEE1 acts on AB at hAB/3 above B and on CD at h1/3 above D (triangular pressure on CD, zero at C). With x = AZ = h2/(tan α2 − tan β2) the horizontal distance between AB and CD, B lies x tan β2 above D, and the moment equation about D is VAB·x = PEE1·(x tan β2 + hAB/3 − h1/3); the weight of ABCD and the equal vertical reaction on BD act on the same line and drop out of the moment. Determine the slip-plane angle α2 of wedge 2, to the nearest degree.

The ground surface rises from C away from the wall at 3 horizontal to 1 vertical (angle β1). The boundary between soil 1 (above) and soil 2 (below) rises from D away from the wall at 6 horizontal to 1 vertical (angle β2). Wedge 2, in soil 2, lies between DE and the slip plane rising from E at angle α2 to point B on the soil boundary; wedge 1, in soil 1, lies between the vertical plane AB and the slip plane rising from B at angle α1 to the ground surface. A is on the ground surface above B; the horizontal distance from AB to the wall is 10/(tan α2 − tan β2); Z is on the vertical through C at the level of A (triangle ACZ). Soil 1: γ1 = 0.12 KCF, Φ1 = 35°, SMF = 2/3, Φd1 = 25°. Soil 2: γ2 = 0.13 KCF, Φ2 = 20°, SMF = 2/3, Φd2 = 13.64°. Slip-plane angle α2 by Eqs. G-25 to G-30 (Appendix G): γ' = 2γ1h1/h2 + γ2 + 2γ1(tan β1 − tan β2)/(tan α2 − tan β2) (G-25); the weight of the surcharge in triangle ACZ Vα = −γ1h2²(tan β1 − tan β2)/[2(tan α2 − tan β2)²] (G-26); A' = tan φd2 − 2Vα(1 + tan² φd2)/(γ'h2²) (G-27); c'1 = [2 tan² φd2 − 4Vα tan β2 (1 + tan² φd2)/(γ'h2²)]/A' (G-28); c'2 = [tan φd2 (1 − tan φd2 tan β2) − tan β2 + 2Vα tan² β2 (1 + tan² φd2)/(γ'h2²)]/A' (G-29); α2 = tan⁻¹[(c'1 + √(c'1² + 4c'2))/2] (G-30). Start from a first trial α2 = 39° and repeat until the trial and computed angles agree; take α2 to the nearest degree and use the rounded α2 in all later steps. Slip-plane angle α1 by Eqs. 3-26 and 3-27 with φd1 and β1: c1 = 2 tan φd1, c2 = 1 − tan φd1 tan β1 − tan β1/tan φd1, α1 = tan⁻¹[(c1 + √(c1² + 4c2))/2]. Coefficients (Appendix H) for each wedge with its own φd, α and β: K = (1 − tan φd cot α)/(1 + tan φd tan α), K1 = K tan α/(tan α − tan β); for wedge 2 also Kv = K tan α. Wedge 1: hAB = h1 + h2(tan β1 − tan β2)/(tan α2 − tan β2); PEE1 = ½K1γ1hAB² on AB, with horizontal pressure pHB = K1γ1hAB at B. Wedge 2: treat the weight of ABCD as a strip surcharge on Surface BD, V = ½(h1 + hAB)(AZ)(γ1) with AZ = h2/(tan α2 − tan β2); Pγ = ½K1γ2h2², PV = KvV, PEE2 = Pγ + PV; the horizontal pressure at D is pHD = K1 (wedge 2) times γ1h1 and at E pHE = 2PEE2/h2 − pHD, linear between D and E. The earth force on AB is transferred to Surface CD by assuming that no shear resistance is developed on Surface BD; moment equilibrium of Block ABCD (about D) then requires equal and opposite vertical shear forces VAB on AB and VCD on CD. PEE1 acts on AB at hAB/3 above B and on CD at h1/3 above D (triangular pressure on CD, zero at C). With x = AZ = h2/(tan α2 − tan β2) the horizontal distance between AB and CD, B lies x tan β2 above D, and the moment equation about D is VAB·x = PEE1·(x tan β2 + hAB/3 − h1/3); the weight of ABCD and the equal vertical reaction on BD act on the same line and drop out of the moment. Determine the strip surcharge V, in kips per foot, the lateral earth force PEE2 on DE, in kips per foot, and the horizontal pressures at D and at E, in ksf.

statement: Find the lateral earth force and pressure distribution on Surfaces FG and HI when: φ = 35°, c = 0, γ = 0.12 kcf, and SMF = 2/3. Figure, driving side: FG is the vertical plane through the heel G of the wall base. The ground at A is hA = 24' above G and 36' horizontally from the plane FG (18' + 18'); it rises at 3 horizontal to 1 vertical to B, 18' from the plane FG and hE = 30' above G; it is level from B to C (12'), then falls at 3 horizontal to 1 vertical from C, 6' from the plane FG, to F on the plane FG, 2' below the level of BC, and on down toward the wall top (4' lower). E is on the plane FG at the level of BC; D is on the plane FG on the extension of AB, hD = 36' above G (6' above E). Lines from G to A and from G to B make 33.69° and 59.036° with the horizontal. Wall base 20' long (11' heel, 3' stem, 6' toe). Resisting side: HI is the vertical plane at the toe end of the base, 20' from G; the ground at I is 3' + 5' above the bottom of the base and falls away from the wall at 4 horizontal to 1 vertical. Driving side, by Eqs. 3-28 to 3-30 with the c terms omitted: A = tan φd − 2V(1 + tan² φd)/(γh²) (Eq. 3-30), c1 = [2 tan² φd − 4V tan β (1 + tan² φd)/(γh²)]/A (Eq. 3-28), c2 = [tan φd (1 − tan φd tan β) − tan β + 2V tan² β (1 + tan² φd)/(γh²)]/A (Eq. 3-29), and α = tan⁻¹[(c1 + √(c1² + 4c2))/2] (Eq. 3-25), with tan φd = (2/3) tan 35°. First assume that the critical slip plane intersects Surface BC (β = 0, h = hE = 30 ft, the weight of the triangular area CEF taken as a negative strip surcharge V); a slip plane meets BC only if α is at least 59.036°. Otherwise assume that it intersects Surface AB (tan β = −1/3, h = hD = 36 ft, the weights of areas BDE and CEF taken as a negative strip surcharge); it does if 33.69° < α < 59.036°. Driving-side coefficients (Appendix H): K = (1 − tan φd cot α)/(1 + tan φd tan α), K1 = K tan α/(tan α − tan β), Kv = K tan α. Pγ = ½K1γhD², PV = KvV, PEE = Pγ + PV. Pressure: the Pγ pressure is K1γ times the depth below D; the (negative) pressure due to PV is a triangle from zero at D to its peak at F, where the net horizontal pressure must equal zero (PV pressure at F = −Pγ pressure at F), and back to zero at the distribution length hv = 2PV/pvF below D. Resisting side by Eqs. 3-35 to 3-38 (passive wedge, no surcharge): A = tan φd (Eq. 3-38), c1 = 2 tan² φd/A (Eq. 3-36), c2 = [tan φd (1 + tan φd tan β) + tan β]/A (Eq. 3-37), α = tan⁻¹[(−c1 + √(c1² + 4c2))/2] (Eq. 3-35), with tan β = −1/4; K = (1 + tan φd cot α)/(1 − tan φd tan α), K1 = K tan α/(tan α − tan β); PEE = ½K1γh² over h = 8 ft, pressure K1γ times the depth below I. Assuming that the critical slip plane intersects Surface BC, determine the slip-plane angle α', in degrees.

statement: Find the lateral earth force and pressure distribution on Surfaces FG and HI when: φ = 35°, c = 0, γ = 0.12 kcf, and SMF = 2/3. Figure, driving side: FG is the vertical plane through the heel G of the wall base. The ground at A is hA = 24' above G and 36' horizontally from the plane FG (18' + 18'); it rises at 3 horizontal to 1 vertical to B, 18' from the plane FG and hE = 30' above G; it is level from B to C (12'), then falls at 3 horizontal to 1 vertical from C, 6' from the plane FG, to F on the plane FG, 2' below the level of BC, and on down toward the wall top (4' lower). E is on the plane FG at the level of BC; D is on the plane FG on the extension of AB, hD = 36' above G (6' above E). Lines from G to A and from G to B make 33.69° and 59.036° with the horizontal. Wall base 20' long (11' heel, 3' stem, 6' toe). Resisting side: HI is the vertical plane at the toe end of the base, 20' from G; the ground at I is 3' + 5' above the bottom of the base and falls away from the wall at 4 horizontal to 1 vertical. Driving side, by Eqs. 3-28 to 3-30 with the c terms omitted: A = tan φd − 2V(1 + tan² φd)/(γh²) (Eq. 3-30), c1 = [2 tan² φd − 4V tan β (1 + tan² φd)/(γh²)]/A (Eq. 3-28), c2 = [tan φd (1 − tan φd tan β) − tan β + 2V tan² β (1 + tan² φd)/(γh²)]/A (Eq. 3-29), and α = tan⁻¹[(c1 + √(c1² + 4c2))/2] (Eq. 3-25), with tan φd = (2/3) tan 35°. First assume that the critical slip plane intersects Surface BC (β = 0, h = hE = 30 ft, the weight of the triangular area CEF taken as a negative strip surcharge V); a slip plane meets BC only if α is at least 59.036°. Otherwise assume that it intersects Surface AB (tan β = −1/3, h = hD = 36 ft, the weights of areas BDE and CEF taken as a negative strip surcharge); it does if 33.69° < α < 59.036°. Driving-side coefficients (Appendix H): K = (1 − tan φd cot α)/(1 + tan φd tan α), K1 = K tan α/(tan α − tan β), Kv = K tan α. Pγ = ½K1γhD², PV = KvV, PEE = Pγ + PV. Pressure: the Pγ pressure is K1γ times the depth below D; the (negative) pressure due to PV is a triangle from zero at D to its peak at F, where the net horizontal pressure must equal zero (PV pressure at F = −Pγ pressure at F), and back to zero at the distribution length hv = 2PV/pvF below D. Resisting side by Eqs. 3-35 to 3-38 (passive wedge, no surcharge): A = tan φd (Eq. 3-38), c1 = 2 tan² φd/A (Eq. 3-36), c2 = [tan φd (1 + tan φd tan β) + tan β]/A (Eq. 3-37), α = tan⁻¹[(−c1 + √(c1² + 4c2))/2] (Eq. 3-35), with tan β = −1/4; K = (1 + tan φd cot α)/(1 − tan φd tan α), K1 = K tan α/(tan α − tan β); PEE = ½K1γh² over h = 8 ft, pressure K1γ times the depth below I. Determine the critical slip-plane angle α on the resisting side, in degrees.

statement: Compute lateral earth pressure using pressure coefficients. Check by wedge method. Figure: BE is the vertical plane through the heel E of the wall base, hB = 24' from B down to E. The ground is level from B to A, 10' from B, then rises away from the wall at 2.5 horizontal to 1 vertical (angle β). C is the point on BE where the extension of the slope through A meets it, 4' below B; hC = 20' from C down to E. BACKFILL: γ = 0.12 KCF, Φ = 35°, c = 0, SMF = 2/3, Φd = tan⁻¹(2/3 tan Φ) = 25°. Critical slip-plane angle: consider the basic wedge to have height hC = 20 ft with a sloping top surface (tan β = 0.4) and take the weight of triangle ABC as a finite surcharge V; then Eqs. 3-28 to 3-30 with the c terms omitted: A = tan φd − 2V(1 + tan² φd)/(γh²) (Eq. 3-30), c1 = [2 tan² φd − 4V tan β (1 + tan² φd)/(γh²)]/A (Eq. 3-28), c2 = [tan φd (1 − tan φd tan β) − tan β + 2V tan² β (1 + tan² φd)/(γh²)]/A (Eq. 3-29), and α = tan⁻¹[(c1 + √(c1² + 4c2))/2] (Eq. 3-25). Pressure by coefficients (Appendix H): K = (1 − tan φd cot α)/(1 + tan φd tan α), K1 = K tan α/(tan α − tan β). Backfill pressure: K1γ times the depth below C (zero at C). Surcharge pressure: a triangle from zero at B to Kγ hBC at C and back to zero at D, where D is on BE at 10 tan α below B (the line at α through A). The combined pressure is their sum. Wedge method, all with the same α: the force on BC from wedge GBC of weight γhBC²/(2 tan α), on BD from wedge ABD of weight ½γ(10)(10 tan α), on BE from wedge FABE of weight γhCE²/[2(tan α − tan β)] + V, each from Eq. 3-23 with c = 0 and no water: P = W(tan α − tan φd)/(1 + tan φd tan α). Pressures at C, D and E follow from these forces with the pressure linear between B, C, D and E: pC = 2PBC/hBC, pD = 2(PBD − PBC)/hCD − pC, pE = 2(PBE − PBD)/hDE − pD. Determine the critical slip-plane angle α, in degrees.

statement: Analyze the wall shown below for stability and bearing capacity. Find the reinforcement required at critical sections. Load Case R1. Given: Backfill: γ = 0.120 kcf, φ = 35°, c = 0. Foundation: γ = 0.135 kcf, φ = 40°, c = 0. Reinforced concrete: γ = 0.150 kcf, f'c = 4 ksi, fy = 48 ksi. All concrete cover = 4.5 in. (to center of gravity of steel). Load factor = 1.9, φ = 0.9. Figure (as read from p. N-3): cantilever wall on a base slab 20.00 ft wide and 3 ft thick. From the backfill (heel) end: heel 12 ft, stem 1.5 ft + 1.5 ft at its base, toe 5 ft. The stem face on the toe side is vertical; the backfill face is battered, so the stem is 1.5 ft wide at the top and 3 ft wide at the base. The stem rises 22 ft above the top of the base slab; the wall is 25 ft high from the base bottom. The foundation ground surface is level with the top of the base slab on both sides; the base bottom is 3 ft below it. The backfill surface rises from the top of the stem away from the wall at a slope of 3 horizontal to 1 vertical. Use the multiple-wedge method of Appendix G with a strength mobilization factor SMF = 2/3: φd = tan⁻¹(2/3 tan φ), rounded to the nearest whole degree as the example does (foundation φd = 29°, backfill φd = 25°). Label the heel end of the base: D at the top of the slab (foundation surface) and E at the base bottom; C on the backfill surface directly above D. The foundation (driving) wedge slip plane rises from E at angle α2 to point B on the foundation surface; A is on the backfill surface directly above B; Surface AB (vertical, through B) carries the backfill force and Surface DE (vertical, 3 ft high) carries the foundation force. Find α2 by iterating Eqs. G-25 to G-30 with the c terms omitted: γ' = 2γ1h1/h2 + γ2 + 2γ1(tan β1 − tan β2)/(tan α2 − tan β2); Vα = γ1h2²(tan β1 − tan β2)/[2(tan α2 − tan β2)²]; A' = tan φd − 2Vα(1 + tan²φd)/(γ'h2²); c1' = [2tan²φd − 4Vα tan β2(1 + tan²φd)/(γ'h2²)]/A'; c2' = [tan φd(1 − tan φd tan β2) − tan β2 + 2Vα tan²β2(1 + tan²φd)/(γ'h2²)]/A'; α2 = tan⁻¹{[c1' + √(c1'² + 4c2')]/2}; with γ1 = 0.120 kcf (backfill), γ2 = 0.135 kcf (foundation), h1 = hCD = 26.5 ft (height of backfill above D), h2 = 3 ft, tan β1 = 1/3, β2 = 0, starting from α2 = 45° + φd/2. hAB = 26.5 + 3 tan β1/tan α2. Backfill slip angle α1 by Eq. 3-25, α1 = tan⁻¹{[c1 + √(c1² + 4c2)]/2}, with c1 = 2 tan φd (Eq. 3-26) and c2 = 1 − tan φd tan β1 − tan β1/tan φd (Eq. 3-27). Earth pressure coefficients (Appendix H): backfill K1 = [(1 − tan φd cot α1)/(1 + tan φd tan α1)]·[tan α1/(tan α1 − tan β1)]; foundation K = (1 − tan φd cot α2)/(1 + tan φd tan α2) and Kv = K tan α2. PAB = ½K1γ1hAB²; PDE = ½Kγ2h2² + KvV, where V = ½(hAB + hCD)γ1(3/tan α2) is the weight of backfill above the foundation wedge; pB = K1γ1hAB; pD = Kγ1hCD; pE = 2PDE/h2 − pD. The structural wedge is the wall plus the soil above the heel, bounded by the vertical plane CD through the heel end. A vertical shear v = (PAB · tan β1)/3 acts downward on plane CD (paragraphs 4-8c, 9-7a). For overturning (paragraph 4-8), PAB acts on plane CD at hCD/3 above the top of the base slab, PDE acts at the centroid of its trapezoidal pressure diagram, soil resistance on the toe side (surface IJ) is neglected, and moments are taken about the toe I (bottom corner of the toe end); xR is the distance of the resultant from I. The base pressure is linear (trapezoidal) with the full base in compression. statement: Analyze the wall below for overturning, sliding and bearing capacity. Case R2, unusual loading condition. Figure (as read from p. N-18): structural wedge b = 30 ft wide (22 ft + 8 ft), base D–E 30 ft. The heel-side face of the structural wedge is the vertical line A–B–C–D through the heel end; the toe-side face is vertical at E–F–G. Toe side: the top of the wall (8 ft wide crest) is 32 ft above the tailwater level G, G is 10 ft above the ground surface F, and F is 6 ft above the base bottom E (48 ft in all). Heel side: the backfill surface rises from the crest away from the wall at slope β = 6 horizontal to 1 vertical and meets the vertical through the heel end at A; the water table B is 22 ft above the ground surface C (β = 0 at C), and C is 6 ft above the base bottom D. Backfill: γm = 0.12 kcf, γs = 0.125 kcf, φ = 35°, c = 0. Rock foundation: γs = 0.140 kcf, φ = 40°, C = 2.5 ksf. Concrete + soil W = 207.61 kips acting 14.70 ft from the toe E. Total seepage path length = 30 ft (along the base D–E). Driving side lateral pressure coefficients with SMF = 2/3 and φd = tan⁻¹(2/3 tan φ). Foundation: K = tan²(45° − φd/2) (Eq. 3-15). Backfill: slip angle α = tan⁻¹{[c1 + √(c1² + 4c2)]/2} (Eq. 3-25) with c1 = 2 tan φd and c2 = 1 − tan φd tan β − tan β/tan φd (Eqs. 3-26, 3-27), tan β = 1/6; K1 = [(1 − tan φd cot α)/(1 + tan φd tan α)]·[tan α/(tan α − tan β)] is used above the water table; below it the buoyant coefficient Kb = K[1 + (tan α/(tan α − tan β) − 1)(γm/γb)] with K = (1 − tan φd cot α)/(1 + tan φd tan α) and γb = γs − γw (Appendix H). The earth pressure on the vertical A–C increases from 0 at A to K1γm hAB at B, then by Kbγb per ft of depth from B to C. There is no earth pressure on Surface CD (the foundation's horizontal pressure at D is negative) and no at-rest pressure on Surface EF. Water: γw = 0.0625 kcf. Rock foundation assumed; since the total seepage path length is the base width, full hydrostatic pressures exist at D (28 ft head) and E (16 ft head) (paragraph 3-22); water on the heel side acts on the vertical through D to a depth of 28 ft and on the toe side through E to a depth of 16 ft. Overturning (paragraph 4-8): the base in compression is 3xR wide from the toe (triangular bearing pressure); full hydrostatic pressure uD acts over the part of the base not in compression and the uplift varies linearly from uD to uE over the compressed width; iterate until the assumed compressed width equals 3xR. Moments about the toe E; xR is measured from E. No vertical shear is applied on the heel plane A–D: the vertical forces are the weight W and the uplift U only (ΣV = W − U). Sliding (paragraph 4-15): T ≤ (N' tan φ + cL)/FS (Eq. 4-12) with N' = ΣV, T = ΣH, φ = 40°, c = 2.5 ksf acting on the compressed length L = 3xR, and the minimum FS = 1.33 (Table 4-1). Bearing (Chapter 5): Q = B̄(ξcd ξci c Nc + ξqd ξqi q0 Nq + ξγd ξγi B̄ γ' Nγ/2) (Eq. 5-2) with δ = tan⁻¹(ΣH/ΣV), e = B/2 − xR, B̄ = B − 2e, D = 6 ft, γ' = 0.140 − 0.0625 kcf, q0 = γ'D (Eq. 5-8a), ξcd = 1 + 0.2(D/B̄)tan(45° + φ/2) (Eq. 5-4a), ξqd = ξγd = 1 + 0.1(D/B̄)tan(45° + φ/2) (Eq. 5-4c), ξqi = ξci = (1 − δ/90)² (Eq. 5-5a), ξγi = (1 − δ/φ)² (Eq. 5-5b), c = 2.5 ksf, Nc = 75.31, Nq = 64.20, Nγ = 93.69 (Table 5-1, φ = 40°), and FS = Q/N' (Eq. 5-1) with N' = ΣV. Determine the developed friction angle φd of the foundation (degrees) and its earth pressure coefficient K (dimensionless).

statement: Analyze the wall below for overturning, sliding and bearing capacity. Case R2, unusual loading condition. Figure (as read from p. N-18): structural wedge b = 30 ft wide (22 ft + 8 ft), base D–E 30 ft. The heel-side face of the structural wedge is the vertical line A–B–C–D through the heel end; the toe-side face is vertical at E–F–G. Toe side: the top of the wall (8 ft wide crest) is 32 ft above the tailwater level G, G is 10 ft above the ground surface F, and F is 6 ft above the base bottom E (48 ft in all). Heel side: the backfill surface rises from the crest away from the wall at slope β = 6 horizontal to 1 vertical and meets the vertical through the heel end at A; the water table B is 22 ft above the ground surface C (β = 0 at C), and C is 6 ft above the base bottom D. Backfill: γm = 0.12 kcf, γs = 0.125 kcf, φ = 35°, c = 0. Rock foundation: γs = 0.140 kcf, φ = 40°, C = 2.5 ksf. Concrete + soil W = 207.61 kips acting 14.70 ft from the toe E. Total seepage path length = 30 ft (along the base D–E). Driving side lateral pressure coefficients with SMF = 2/3 and φd = tan⁻¹(2/3 tan φ). Foundation: K = tan²(45° − φd/2) (Eq. 3-15). Backfill: slip angle α = tan⁻¹{[c1 + √(c1² + 4c2)]/2} (Eq. 3-25) with c1 = 2 tan φd and c2 = 1 − tan φd tan β − tan β/tan φd (Eqs. 3-26, 3-27), tan β = 1/6; K1 = [(1 − tan φd cot α)/(1 + tan φd tan α)]·[tan α/(tan α − tan β)] is used above the water table; below it the buoyant coefficient Kb = K[1 + (tan α/(tan α − tan β) − 1)(γm/γb)] with K = (1 − tan φd cot α)/(1 + tan φd tan α) and γb = γs − γw (Appendix H). The earth pressure on the vertical A–C increases from 0 at A to K1γm hAB at B, then by Kbγb per ft of depth from B to C. There is no earth pressure on Surface CD (the foundation's horizontal pressure at D is negative) and no at-rest pressure on Surface EF. Water: γw = 0.0625 kcf. Rock foundation assumed; since the total seepage path length is the base width, full hydrostatic pressures exist at D (28 ft head) and E (16 ft head) (paragraph 3-22); water on the heel side acts on the vertical through D to a depth of 28 ft and on the toe side through E to a depth of 16 ft. Overturning (paragraph 4-8): the base in compression is 3xR wide from the toe (triangular bearing pressure); full hydrostatic pressure uD acts over the part of the base not in compression and the uplift varies linearly from uD to uE over the compressed width; iterate until the assumed compressed width equals 3xR. Moments about the toe E; xR is measured from E. No vertical shear is applied on the heel plane A–D: the vertical forces are the weight W and the uplift U only (ΣV = W − U). Sliding (paragraph 4-15): T ≤ (N' tan φ + cL)/FS (Eq. 4-12) with N' = ΣV, T = ΣH, φ = 40°, c = 2.5 ksf acting on the compressed length L = 3xR, and the minimum FS = 1.33 (Table 4-1). Bearing (Chapter 5): Q = B̄(ξcd ξci c Nc + ξqd ξqi q0 Nq + ξγd ξγi B̄ γ' Nγ/2) (Eq. 5-2) with δ = tan⁻¹(ΣH/ΣV), e = B/2 − xR, B̄ = B − 2e, D = 6 ft, γ' = 0.140 − 0.0625 kcf, q0 = γ'D (Eq. 5-8a), ξcd = 1 + 0.2(D/B̄)tan(45° + φ/2) (Eq. 5-4a), ξqd = ξγd = 1 + 0.1(D/B̄)tan(45° + φ/2) (Eq. 5-4c), ξqi = ξci = (1 − δ/90)² (Eq. 5-5a), ξγi = (1 − δ/φ)² (Eq. 5-5b), c = 2.5 ksf, Nc = 75.31, Nq = 64.20, Nγ = 93.69 (Table 5-1, φ = 40°), and FS = Q/N' (Eq. 5-1) with N' = ΣV. Determine the backfill slip-plane angle α (degrees) and the coefficient K1 above the water table (dimensionless).

statement: Analyze the wall for overturning stability, sliding and bearing capacity. Determine water pressure using the line of creep method. Calculate reinforcement required at critical sections. Case I1, design flood. Figure (as read from p. N-24): base slab 20 ft wide (riverside end to point G): heel 12 ft, stem 0.5 ft + 1.5 ft, toe 6 ft; the slab is 2 ft thick, tapering to 1.5 ft at the landside end; its top is 3 ft below the ground surface B–H and its bottom (line E–G) 5 ft below it. The stem top A is 17 ft above the base bottom. The riverside water surface is 9 ft above the ground surface and 3 ft below A. A key below the riverside end of the base extends 4 ft below the base bottom: 2 ft wide at the base bottom (from the riverside face to E) and 1.5 ft wide at its bottom (C–D), riverside face vertical. Landside groundwater at the ground surface H, directly above G. Wt. of concrete, water & soil above CDEG = 25.37 kips acting 11.12 ft from G. Para. 7-6: assumed crack along the riverside face to the bottom of the key (B to C). Seepage path for sliding and overturning analysis: C straight to G, then G up to H. Check sliding on these planes: CG (straight from C to G) and CF (horizontal at the level of C, to F directly below G). Soil properties: γSAT = 0.12 kcf; c = 0.9 ksf, φ = 0 (undrained); φ = 28°, c = 0 (drained). Line of creep (paragraph 3-19): γw = 0.0625 kcf; LCG = √(4² + 20²), LBC = 0 (crack), LGH = 5 ft, LS = LCG + LGH, head differential Δh = 9 ft; pressure at a point = γw × (depth below headwater − Δh × creep length to the point/LS). For D and E prorate the head loss along CG, Δh LCG/LS, along the concrete surface C–D–E–G (LCD = 1.5 ft, LDE = √(4² + 0.5²), LEG = 18 ft). Overturning (paragraph 4-8) on the free body above C–D–E–G, moments about G: uplift along C–D–E–G from the line-of-creep pressures, acting on the horizontal projections; riverside water on the vertical through C to its full 18 ft depth; on the landside, the horizontal water force on the key face DE (line-of-creep pressures uE to uD over its 4 ft height) plus the water on the vertical GH (linear from 0 at H to uG at G). Soil resistance above G is neglected; the landside soil force below G is just sufficient to make ΣH = 0 and acts uniformly over the 4 ft from G down to the level of C (resultant 2 ft below G). xR is measured from G. Sliding (paragraph 4-10) on plane CG, inclined at α = tan⁻¹(4/20): the free body includes the saturated soil between the base and plane CG (outside the key); the uplift on CG varies linearly from uC to uG; its vertical component acts on the 20 ft horizontal projection and its horizontal component on the 4 ft vertical projection, the latter added to the landside water on GH; no landside soil resistance. N' = ΣV cos α + ΣH sin α, T = ΣH cos α − ΣV sin α; T ≤ (N' tan φ + cL)/FS (Eq. 4-12) with the minimum FS = 1.5 (Table 4-2): undrained c = 0.9 ksf on L = LCG with φ = 0; drained φ = 28°, c = 0. Sliding on plane CF (horizontal at the level of C): seepage path LS = LCF + LFH = 20 ft + 9 ft; uplift linear from uC to uF over 20 ft; soil between the base and CF included; landside water on FH linear from 0 at H to uF at F; landside soil resistance PR on FH with effective weight γ' = (9 ft × 0.12 − uF)/9 and h = 9 ft. Undrained: cd = SMF × c with SMF = 2/3 (Eq. 3-10), K0 = 1.0 (Eq. 3-4), PR = ½K0γ'h², resistance cd LCF. Drained: K = ½Kp (paragraph 3-8b) with Kp = tan²(45° + φ/2), φ = 28°, PR = ½Kγ'h², resistance N' tan φ with N' = ΣV. FS = 1.5. Bearing (on plane CG): load inclination δ = tan⁻¹(T/N') with the plane-CG forces (Figure 5-1). Determine the line-of-creep water pressures uC, uG, uD and uE, in ksf.

N-24): base slab 20 ft wide (riverside end to point G): heel 12 ft, stem 0.5 ft + 1.5 ft, toe 6 ft; the slab is 2 ft thick, tapering to 1.5 ft at the landside end; its top is 3 ft below the ground surface B–H and its bottom (line E–G) 5 ft below it. The stem top A is 17 ft above the base bottom. The riverside water surface is 9 ft above the ground surface and 3 ft below A. A key below the riverside end of the base extends 4 ft below the base bottom: 2 ft wide at the base bottom (from the riverside face to E) and 1.5 ft wide at its bottom (C–D), riverside face vertical. Landside groundwater at the ground surface H, directly above G. Wt. of concrete, water & soil above CDEG = 25.37 kips acting 11.12 ft from G. Para. 7-6: assumed crack along the riverside face to the bottom of the key (B to C). Seepage path for sliding and overturning analysis: C straight to G, then G up to H. Check sliding on these planes: CG (straight from C to G) and CF (horizontal at the level of C, to F directly below G). Soil properties: γSAT = 0.12 kcf; c = 0.9 ksf, φ = 0 (undrained); φ = 28°, c = 0 (drained). Line of creep (paragraph 3-19): γw = 0.0625 kcf; LCG = √(4² + 20²), LBC = 0 (crack), LGH = 5 ft, LS = LCG + LGH, head differential Δh = 9 ft; pressure at a point = γw × (depth below headwater − Δh × creep length to the point/LS). For D and E prorate the head loss along CG, Δh LCG/LS, along the concrete surface C–D–E–G (LCD = 1.5 ft, LDE = √(4² + 0.5²), LEG = 18 ft). Overturning (paragraph 4-8) on the free body above C–D–E–G, moments about G: uplift along C–D–E–G from the line-of-creep pressures, acting on the horizontal projections; riverside water on the vertical through C to its full 18 ft depth; on the landside, the horizontal water force on the key face DE (line-of-creep pressures uE to uD over its 4 ft height) plus the water on the vertical GH (linear from 0 at H to uG at G). Soil resistance above G is neglected; the landside soil force below G is just sufficient to make ΣH = 0 and acts uniformly over the 4 ft from G down to the level of C (resultant 2 ft below G). xR is measured from G. Sliding (paragraph 4-10) on plane CG, inclined at α = tan⁻¹(4/20): the free body includes the saturated soil between the base and plane CG (outside the key); the uplift on CG varies linearly from uC to uG; its vertical component acts on the 20 ft horizontal projection and its horizontal component on the 4 ft vertical projection, the latter added to the landside water on GH; no landside soil resistance. N' = ΣV cos α + ΣH sin α, T = ΣH cos α − ΣV sin α; T ≤ (N' tan φ + cL)/FS (Eq. 4-12) with the minimum FS = 1.5 (Table 4-2): undrained c = 0.9 ksf on L = LCG with φ = 0; drained φ = 28°, c = 0. Sliding on plane CF (horizontal at the level of C): seepage path LS = LCF + LFH = 20 ft + 9 ft; uplift linear from uC to uF over 20 ft; soil between the base and CF included; landside water on FH linear from 0 at H to uF at F; landside soil resistance PR on FH with effective weight γ' = (9 ft × 0.12 − uF)/9 and h = 9 ft. Undrained: cd = SMF × c with SMF = 2/3 (Eq. 3-10), K0 = 1.0 (Eq. 3-4), PR = ½K0γ'h², resistance cd LCF. Drained: K = ½Kp (paragraph 3-8b) with Kp = tan²(45° + φ/2), φ = 28°, PR = ½Kγ'h², resistance N' tan φ with N' = ΣV. FS = 1.5. Bearing (on plane CG): load inclination δ = tan⁻¹(T/N') with the plane-CG forces (Figure 5-1). On plane CG, determine the normal force N' and the shear force T, in kips per ft.

statement: Analyze the wall for overturning, sliding and bearing capacity. Use the line of creep method to determine water pressures. Load Case I1, Design Flood. Calculate reinforcement at critical sections. Figure (as read from p. N-41): base 16 ft long horizontally (riverside end C to landside end D): heel 8 ft, stem 0.5 ft + 1.5 ft (vertical stem), toe 6 ft. The base bottom is a plane C–D inclined at α = 14.04°, C 4 ft below D; the slab is 1.5 ft thick at both ends. The stem top A is 3 ft above the riverside water surface, which is 10 ft above the riverside ground surface B; B is 7 ft above C. On the landside, A is 13 ft above the ground surface E, landside groundwater is at E, and E is 3 ft above D. Water, soil & concrete: 19.17 kips acting 9.35 ft (horizontally) from D. Crack (para. 7-6) along the riverside end from B to C. γSAT = 0.12 kcf, φ = 0, c = 0.9 ksf. Line of creep (paragraph 3-19): γw = 0.0625 kcf; the crack B–C carries the full headwater pressure down to C; the seepage path runs from C along the base to D and up to E (LS = LCD + LDE, LDE = 3 ft); head differential Δh = 10 ft (headwater to landside groundwater at E); the pressure at a point is γw times its depth below the headwater less the head lost along the creep path to it, the head loss being prorated by creep length. Overturning on the free body above plane CD, moments about D (paragraph 4-8): uplift linear from uC to uD on the 16 ft horizontal projection; riverside water on the vertical through C to its full 17 ft depth; landside horizontal water = water on DE (linear from 0 at E to uD at D) plus the horizontal component of the base water pressure on CD (uD to uC over its 4 ft vertical projection); soil resistance above D is neglected. N' = ΣV cos α + ΣH sin α, T = ΣH cos α − ΣV sin α, and xR = M_D/N' measured along CD from D. Sliding on Surface CD (paragraph 4-15): T ≤ (N' tan φ + cL)/FS (Eq. 4-12) with φ = 0, c = 0.9 ksf, L = LCD and the minimum FS = 1.5 (Table 4-2). Bearing (Chapter 5, Eq. 5-2) on CD: Q = B̄(ξcd ξci ξct ξcg c Nc + ξqd ξqi ξqt ξqg q0 Nq + ξγd ξγi ξγt ξγg B̄ γ' Nγ/2) with δ = tan⁻¹(T/N'), e = LCD/2 − xR, B̄ = LCD − 2e, D = 3 ft, γ' = γsat − γw, q0 = γ'D (Eq. 5-8a), ξcd = 1 + 0.2(D/B̄) (Eq. 5-4a), ξqd = ξγd = 1.00 (Eq. 5-4b), ξci = ξqi = (1 − δ/90)² (Eq. 5-5a), ξγi = 0, ξqt = ξγt = 1, ξct = 1 − 2α/(π + 2) with α in radians (Eq. 5-6b), ground slope factors ξg = 1 (β = 0), Nc = 5.14, Nq = 1, Nγ = 0 (Table 5-1), and FS = Q/N' (Eq. 5-1). Determine the water pressures uC and uD, in ksf.

statement: Analyze the wall for overturning, sliding and bearing capacity. Determine water pressure using the line of creep method. Load Case I2. Assume that sheet pile cutoff wall is 50 percent effective. Figure (as read from p. N-52): base b = 18 ft (riverside end C to landside end F): heel 10 ft, stem 0.5 ft + 1.5 ft, toe 6 ft; base 2 ft thick. The riverside water surface is at the stem top A, 12 ft above the riverside ground surface B, which is 4 ft above the top of the base (18 ft from A to the base bottom). On the landside the tailwater is 12 ft below A, the ground surface G is 2 ft below the tailwater and 2 ft above the top of the base (A is 16 ft above the top of the base). Steel sheet piling at D, 0.75 ft from the riverside end C, extends 24 ft below the base bottom to an impervious stratum E (see paragraph 7-4a regarding penetration of impervious stratum below pervious soil). Assumed crack along the riverside end from B to C. Soil + water + conc. = 24.62 kips acting 10.11 ft from the toe F. Soil properties: γSAT = 0.125 kcf, φ = 20°, c = 0.4 ksf. Water pressure with the sheet pile cutoff (paragraph 7-4a), γw = 0.0625 kcf: the headwater side of the sheet pile carries the full headwater pressure; the pressure at F is found by the line of creep along the seepage path from the cutoff (D) along the base to F and up to G (head differential = headwater to tailwater); because the cutoff is only 50 percent effective, the pressure on its tailwater side at D is reduced from the full-head value by half of the difference between the full-head value and the pressure at F. Uplift: full head over C–D (0.75 ft), then linear from the D value to the F value over D–F. statement: Analyze the wall for overturning, sliding and bearing capacity. Load Case C2b, breaking wave condition. Figure (as read from p. N-63): base 22 ft long (riverside end C to landside end D): heel 15 ft, stem 1.5 ft + 0.5 ft (landside face battered at its lower part), toe 5 ft; the slab is 1.5 ft thick at both ends and 2.0 ft at the stem. The ground surface on both sides (B riverside, E landside) is 7 ft above the base bottom (5.0 ft + 2.0 ft); the stem top A is 8.5 ft above the ground surface E (15.5 ft above the base bottom). The still water level (S.W.L.) is 3.7 ft above B; the top of wave is 6.5 ft above B; landside water at E. Assumed crack along the riverside end from B to C. Soil + water + conc. = 28.61 kips acting 11.39 ft from D. Soil properties: γSAT = 0.125 kcf, φ = 0°, c = 0.90 ksf. Water: γW = 0.064 kcf. Water pressures (paragraphs 3-19 and 3-24d,f): seepage from the still water level (swl), by the line of creep; the crack B–C carries full hydrostatic pressure from the swl; the creep path runs from C along the base to D (LCD = 22 ft) and up to E (LDE = 7.0 ft); the pressure is zero at E (end of creep, tail water); the head differential is the swl height above the landside water at E. Wave force (paragraph 3-24): the increase in static force due to the wave crest is the hydrostatic force on the vertical through C with water up to the top of wave, less the hydrostatic force with water up to the swl, acting at the moment centroid of that difference; the static water force on the riverside is the hydrostatic force on the vertical through C with water up to the swl; the dynamic force of the breaking wave, from Chapter 7 of the Shore Protection Manual, is 5.176 kips acting at the swl. Soil force, resisting side: K0 = 1.00 (at-rest), γ' = γsat − seepage uplift = [7(0.125) − uD] ÷ 7, P0 = ½K0γ'h² with h = 7 ft, at h/3; landside water on the vertical through D, linear from 0 at E to uD at D. Overturning (paragraph 4-8): initially all of the base is assumed in compression; full hydrostatic uplift uC is applied to any part of the base not in compression, and over the compressed width a = 3xR (from the toe D) the uplift varies linearly from uC to uD; the percent of the base in compression is recomputed until the assumed value equals the computed one. Moments about D. Sliding (paragraph 4-15): Eq. 4-12, T ≤ (N' tan φ + cL)/FS, with N' = ΣV, T = ΣH, φ = 0, c = 0.9 ksf on L = a, and the minimum FS = 1.25 (Table 4-3). Bearing (Chapter 5): Q = B̄(ξcd ξci c Nc + ξqd ξqi q0 Nq) (Eq. 5-2) with δ = tan⁻¹(ΣH/ΣV), e = B/2 − xR, B̄ = B − 2e, D = 7 ft, γb = 0.125 − 0.064 kcf, q0 = γbD (Eq. 5-8a), ξcd = 1 + 0.2(D/B̄) (Eq. 5-4a), ξqd = 1.00 (Eq. 5-4b), ξci = ξqi = (1 − δ/90)² (Eq. 5-5a), Nc = 5.14, Nq = 1.00 (Table 5-1), and FS = Q/N' (Eq. 5-1) with N' = ΣV. Determine the water pressures uB, uC and uD, in ksf.

statement: Figure 10-5 shows the idealized subsurface profile (Step 1), soil properties (Step 3), and trial dimensions of a drilled shaft (Step 4) under consideration for a bridge project. Calculate the nominal side resistance for the two layers of silty sand extending to a depth of 33 ft using the β-method as described above. [Figure 10-5: Layer 1, silty sand (SM) from the ground surface to a depth of 15 ft, N60 = 9, (N1)60 = 14, γ = 115 pcf; groundwater table at a depth of 15 ft; Layer 2, silty sand (SM) from 15 to 33 ft, N60 = 27, (N1)60 = 28, γsat = 125 pcf; Layer 3, stiff clay (CL) from 33 to 60 ft, mean su = 2,000 psf based on lab UU tests, γ = 125 pcf; trial drilled shaft of diameter B = 5 ft extending to a depth of 60 ft.] Illustrative Example 10-5 (Perform Strength Limit State Check for Axial Design): For the trial design presented in Illustrative Example 10-1 and depicted in Figure 10-5, the nominal resistances were calculated in Illustrative Examples 10-1, 10-2 and 10-3. Information provided by the structural engineer includes a governing factored axial load demand corresponding to the Strength I limit state load combination: Σ γQ = 766 kips. Based on the calculated resistances, determine whether the trial design satisfies the LRFD criterion. Use the β-method as applied in the example. For each sand layer: φ' = δ = 27.5 + 9.2 log[(N1)60] (base-10 logarithm, Chen and Kulhawy, 2002); preconsolidation stress σ'p = pa × 0.47 (N60)^m (Eq. 10-11) with m = 0.8 for silty sand and pa = 2,116 psf; OCR = σ'p/σ'v (Eq. 10-9), with σ'v the vertical effective stress at mid-depth of the layer; Ko = (1 − sin φ') OCR^(sin φ') ≤ Kp (Eq. 10-8), with K = Ko (no change of horizontal stress from construction); β = K tan δ (Eq. 10-6); unit side resistance fSN = σ'v β (Eq. 10-7); nominal side resistance of the layer RSN = π B Δz fSN (Eq. 10-5), Δz the layer thickness. Take the unit weight of water as 62.4 pcf. For the Illustrative Example 10-5 check use the resistance factors of Table 8-4: φ = 0.55 for side resistance in cohesionless soil, φ = 0.45 for side resistance in cohesive soil and φ = 0.40 for base resistance in cohesive soil. The clay layer (Layer 3) provides the nominal side resistance RSN,3 = 479.7 kips (Illustrative Example 10-2) and the nominal base resistance RBN,3 = 453.6 kips (Illustrative Example 10-3). The factored resistance is Σ φi Ri = Σ φS,i RSN,i + φB RBN (Eq. 10-2), and the capacity to demand ratio is C/D = Σ φi Ri / Σ γQ. Determine the Rankine passive earth pressure coefficient Kp of Layer 1 and of Layer 2, against which Ko is checked (dimensionless).

statement: Given: The proposed embankment geometry as shown in Figure A.5-2 and the embankment and foundation soil properties at the east approach as provided in Table A.5-1. Assume that the shallow (≈ 3′) surface layer of organic material shown in the idealized soil profile (Figure A.4-2) has been removed and replaced with select material having the same properties as the embankment fill. Required: Perform hand calculations based on the Ordinary Method of Slices to compute the minimum factor of safety of the I-0 approach embankment at the east abutment. Compare the minimum factor of safety obtained from the hand calculations with the minimum factors of safety obtained from computer analyses based on the Ordinary Method of Slices and Bishop's Method. Perform hand calculations based on the sliding (Rankine) block method to compute the minimum factor of safety of the I-0 approach embankment at the east abutment and compare the result with the results obtained from the two circular arc type failure analyses. statement: Given: The subsurface profile and soil properties shown below. Required: Determine the allowable pile capacity using static analysis. (Profile as drawn: at the pier, sand γ = 110 pcf, φ = 36° from the ground surface to 15 ft, with the water table 10 ft below the ground surface and the pier footing base 4 ft below the ground surface, leaving 11 ft of sand below the footing; clay γ = 125 pcf, c = 1,100 psf (assume sensitivity = 2), 25 ft thick; gravel γ = 130 pcf, φ = 43°, 10 ft thick. At the East Abutment, fill γ = 130 pcf, φ = 40°, 23 ft high, over 7 ft of the sand, 35 ft of the clay and 10 ft of the gravel.) Pile alternatives: a 12 inch diameter closed end pipe pile (70-ton design load) and a 12 inch H-pile, HP 12x84 (120-ton design load). Pipe pile: V = 0.785 ft3/ft, toe area Ap = 0.785 ft2, perimeter Cd = π d = 3.14 ft. H-pile: V = 0.17 ft3/ft, Ap = 24.6 in2, Cd = 4 ft. Soil resistance to driving SRD = shaft resistance above the clay + clay shaft resistance divided by the sensitivity + the required ultimate capacity (design load × SF, SF = 2) developed below the clay. Take 1 ton = 2,000 lbs and 1 kip = 1,000 lbs. Use the Nordlund method for shaft resistance in granular soil, Rs = Kδ CF pd Cd (sin δ) D (Equation 9-6), with φ limited to 36° for skin friction in the gravel and the fill; adhesion ca ≈ c = 1,100 psf (α ≈ 1.0) in the clay, Rs = ca Cd D; toe resistance Rt = Ap αt pt N′q (Equation 9-7a), limited by Rt(max) = qL Ap (Equation 9-7b). Values as applied in the example. Pipe pile: δ/φ = 0.6 (Figure 9-7), Kδ = 1.92 (Table 9-6(a)), CF = 0.75 (Figure 9-12) in the sand and fill and CF = 0.7 in the gravel. H-pile: δ/φ = 0.80, Kδ = 1.30, CF = 0.92. Pier toe in gravel (φ = 43°): αt ≈ 0.75 (Figure 9-13(a)), N′q = 300 (Figure 9-13(b)), limiting pt max = 3,000 psf, qL = 680 ksf (Figure 9-14). Effective overburden pd read from the po diagram: pier sand average (at 9.5 ft) 1,050 psf; top of the gravel at the pier 3,200 psf; abutment, pipe pile: fill 1,650 psf, sand 3,330 psf; abutment, H-pile: fill 1,495 psf, sand 3,303 psf, gravel 5,600 psf; at a tip depth of 23 ft in the fill 2,990 psf, with αt = 0.74 and N′q = 170 there and a limiting unit toe resistance of 200 tsf. Further conventions as applied in the example. For the trial 4 ft embedment in the gravel at the pier, the gravel shaft segment uses pd = 3,200 psf (the value at the top of the gravel) for both piles; the limiting pt max = 3,000 psf applies only to the toe pt. For the H-pile, CF = 0.92 in every granular layer, including the gravel. For a pile tip embedded 23 ft in the fill, SRD(fill) = Rs over the 23 ft of fill + Rt at the tip. For the abutment H-pile, the total shaft resistance is the sum of the fill, sand, clay and gravel shaft resistances with the clay term taken as the clay shaft resistance divided by the sensitivity (the same clay value used in the SRD). For the abutment H-pile with its tip embedded 23 ft in the fill, determine the toe resistance Rt from Equation 9-7a and the soil resistance to driving SRD(fill), in tons.

statement: Figure 21, Example of Analysis of Anchored Bulkhead. A sheet pile bulkhead is restrained by an anchor (tie rod) 6 ft below the top of the backfill (point A). Surcharges on the backfill: a uniform q = 300 PSF and a line load QL = 5,000 PLF at 3 ft from the wall. Upper soil, from the top (A) to point C 24 ft below the top: φ1 = 25°, c1 = 100 PSF, γT = 115 PCF. Lower soil, below C: φ2 = 35°, c2 = 50 PSF, γT = 130 PCF. The water level behind the wall is 5 ft below the top (point B); the outside water level is 2.5 ft lower. The dredge line (point D) is 6 ft below C, so H = 30 ft, and the sheeting toe (point E) is 14 ft below the dredge line. Moment reduction: assume fs = 27,000 PSI, E = 30,000,000 PSI; try ZP 32, I = 385.7 IN⁴, S = 38.3 IN³. Values read in the example: KA = .41 for the upper soil and KA = .27 for the lower soil (Figure 3); Kp = 6.0 for the lower soil (Figure 5); wall friction δ = 14° (Table 1); line-load resultant PH = 0.55 QL (Figure 11, m = x/H = 0.1) acting at R = 0.60H above the dredge line; and, for the trial section, Mdesign/Mmax = 0.83 (Figure 19). Active pressure including the uniform surcharge: σH = σv KA − 2c√KA (Figure 2), negative values taken as zero; passive pressure σH = γz Kp + 2c√Kp. Below the water the example uses submerged unit weights of .053 KCF (upper soil) and .068 KCF (lower soil), with γw = .0625 KCF; the net water pressure is γw × 2.5 ft. Safety factor against toe failure: take moments about the anchor A, Fs = Σ moments of passive forces / Σ moments of active forces. Anchor pull: Ap = ΣPA − ΣPp/Fs with Fs = 2.5. Maximum bending moment at the point of zero shear, located at depth X below the outside water level. Moment reduction by Rowe's flexibility number ρ = (H + D)⁴/(EI), with H + D in inches (Figure 19). Resultant forces as labelled in Figure 21, with their lever arms about the anchor A used in the safety factor: PA1 = 1.55 KIP (0.73 ft), PH = 2.75 KIP (6 ft), PA2 = 10.4 KIP (10.52 ft), PA3 = 4.05 KIP (21.09 ft), PA4 = 10.9 KIP (31.0 ft), Pp1 = 43.26 KIP (33.3 ft). In the bending-moment computation the example places PA1 2.1 ft above the outside water level. Anchor pull: ΣPA = PA1 + PH + PA2 + PA3 + PA4 (all five labelled active forces, the line-load resultant PH included; the net water pressure is part of the labelled forces and is not added separately) and ΣPp = Pp1. Point of zero shear: at depth X below the outside water level the shear is Ap − PA1 − PH − (resultant of the net pressure between the outside water level and X) = 0, where PA1 stands for all pressure above the outside water level, PH (12 ft deep, 4.5 ft below the outside water level) lies above X, and the net pressure below the outside water level is the active pressure of the upper soil plus the constant net water pressure γw × 2.5 ft. Mmax is the moment of these same loads (Ap, PA1, PH and the net pressure above X) about the point of zero shear. Determine the active earth pressure σH at point C in the upper soil, in ksf.

The footing, with plan dimensions B = 9.5 ft by L = 14.25 ft, rests 5 ft below grade. Loads at the base: 189 kips vertical together with M = 233 kip-ft bending the footing about its long axis. For the eccentric load take e = M/P and B′ = B − 2e, L as built. Surcharge from the moist γ; under the base γ is a three-case value: buoyant γ_sat − 62.4 pcf (z_w < D), linear in (z_w − D)/B′ (D ≤ z_w ≤ D + B′), moist γ (z_w > D + B′). Take Brinch Hansen's shape factors, s_γ = 1 − 0.4 B′/L; s_q = 1 + sin φ′ × B′/L, with N_γ = (3/2)(N_q − 1) tan φ′.

Find the reduced width B_eff (ft), q_ult as the gross limit unit bearing capacity (ksf) and the limit load Q_ult in kips on the effective area. Neglect depth and inclination factors.

The groundwater level is at depth 7.1 ft below grade. Clean medium dense sand lies throughout (c′ = 0, φ′ 35°); γ = 126 pcf above the water table and γ_sat = 131 pcf below it.

A rectangular footing 9 ft wide and 13.5 ft long has its underside 2.5 ft down. The column brings P = 144 kips with 143 kip-ft of moment in the direction of B.

Neglect depth and inclination factors. Use effective dimensions, B′ = B − 2e with e = M/P, L unchanged. Use the Brinch Hansen shape set on B′/L, s_q = (B′ sin φ′)/L + 1; s_γ = −0.4 B′/L + 1, and N_γ = (N_q − 1) × 1.5 tan φ′. Above the base the moist γ applies; the γ term takes γ_sat − 62.4 pcf for water above the base (z_w < D), the moist γ for water deeper than D + B′, and the straight line γ_b + (z_w − D)(γ − γ_b)/B′ between. Determine the reduced width B_eff (ft), the gross limit unit bearing capacity q_ult in ksf and Q_ult over B′ L, in kips.

The site is underlain by medium dense sand without cohesion, effective φ′ 34° and no cohesion; unit weights 120 pcf (moist) and 129 pcf (saturated). The groundwater level is at depth 6.4 ft below grade.

A rectangular footing 6 ft wide and 9 ft long sits at depth 4.5 ft. Loads at the base: 103 kips vertical and a moment M = 87 kip-ft that acts across the width B (about the long axis). Carry the moment through e = M/P, B′ = B − 2e and L′ = L. Use the Brinch Hansen shape set on B′/L, s_γ = 1 − 0.4 B′/L; s_q = 1 + B′ sin φ′ / L, with N_γ = 1.5(N_q − 1) tan φ′. The surcharge uses the moist γ; under the base γ is by z_w: if z_w < D the buoyant γ_sat − 62.4 pcf; if D ≤ z_w ≤ D + B′ linear interpolation to the moist γ at D + B′; if deeper, the moist γ.

Find B_eff in feet, q_ult, the gross limit unit bearing capacity of the effective area (ksf), plus the load Q_ult = q_ult B′ L in kips. Neglect depth and inclination factors.

With B = 8.5 ft and L = 12.75 ft, the footing sits at depth 3.5 ft. The site is underlain by medium dense sand without cohesion (c′ = 0, φ′ 35°); γ_sat = 131 pcf under water, γ = 129 pcf above. Standpipes show groundwater 5 ft down. From the column come 92 kips and a moment of 47 kip-ft about the footing's long axis, tilting the resultant across B.

Effective area first: B′ = B − 2e with e = M/P, L unchanged. Use the Brinch Hansen shape set on B′/L, s_q equal to one plus (B′/L) sin φ′; s_γ = 1 − 0.4 × (B′/L), together with N_γ = (3/2)(N_q − 1) tan φ′. Above the base the moist γ applies; below the base take γ as γ_b + [(z_w − D)/B′](γ − γ_b) with γ_b = γ_sat − 62.4 pcf, used only for D ≤ z_w ≤ D + B′ (γ_b itself if z_w < D, the moist γ if z_w > D + B′). Report three values: B_eff (ft), q_ult as the gross limit unit bearing capacity (ksf) and the limit load Q_ult in kips on the effective area. Neglect depth and inclination factors.

Water was met 8.7 ft beneath the surface, all year. The footing bears on medium dense sand, friction angle 34°; γ_sat = 127 pcf under water, γ = 120 pcf above.

With B = 8 ft and L = 16 ft, the footing sits at depth 4.5 ft. The base receives 85 kips of vertical load and a moment of 41 kip-ft about the footing's long axis, tilting the resultant across B.

Neglect depth and inclination factors. Meyerhof's effective footing applies: B′ = B − 2M/P (L is not reduced). Shape factors are Brinch Hansen's on the effective plan, s_q = 1 + (B′/L) sin φ′; s_γ = 1 − 0.4 B′/L, with N_γ = 1.5(N_q − 1) tan φ′. The surcharge uses the moist γ; under the base γ is γ_sat − 62.4 pcf for water above the base (z_w < D), the moist γ for water deeper than D + B′, and the straight line γ_b + (z_w − D)(γ − γ_b)/B′ between. Determine the reduced width B_eff (ft), q_ult as the gross limit unit bearing capacity (ksf) and Q_ult = q_ult B′ L (kips).

Required: B_eff in feet, the effective area's gross limit unit bearing capacity q_ult (ksf) and the limit load Q_ult in kips on the effective area. Replace the footing by its effective rectangle: e = M/P, B′ = B − 2e and L′ = L. The surcharge uses the moist γ; for the weight term use by z_w: if z_w < D the buoyant γ_sat − 62.4 pcf; if D ≤ z_w ≤ D + B′ linear interpolation to the moist γ at D + B′; if deeper, the moist γ. Shape factors are Brinch Hansen's on the effective plan, s_γ = 1 − 2B′/(5L); s_q = 1 + sin φ′ × B′/L, together with N_γ = 1.5 tan φ′ (N_q − 1).

The footing bears on medium dense sand (c′ = 0, φ′ 34°); unit weights 117 pcf (moist) and 127 pcf (saturated). Seasonal readings keep the water table 12.6 ft below the ground surface. The base, 9 ft by 13.5 ft in plan, rests 4.5 ft below grade. Loads at the base: 110 kips vertical with 109 kip-ft of moment in the direction of B. Neglect depth and inclination factors.

Tests were run on the medium dense clean sand with φ′ = 36°; unit weights 128 pcf (moist) and 131 pcf (saturated). Monitoring wells place the water 11.9 ft below the ground surface.

The planned footing measures 10 ft x 15 ft and bears at 3.5 ft beneath the surface. The column brings P = 72 kips and a moment M = 86 kip-ft that acts across the width B (about the long axis). Carry the moment through B′ = B − 2e with e = M/P, L unchanged. Take Brinch Hansen's shape factors, s_γ equal to one less 0.4 B′/L; s_q = (B′ sin φ′)/L + 1, together with N_γ = 1.5 × tan φ′ × (N_q − 1). The surcharge uses the moist γ; under the base γ is the moist γ when z_w > D + B′, γ_b + (γ − γ_b)(z_w − D)/B′ when D ≤ z_w ≤ D + B′, and γ_b = γ_sat − 62.4 pcf when z_w < D.

Find three values: B_eff (ft), the effective area's gross limit unit bearing capacity q_ult (ksf) and the limit load Q_ult in kips on the effective area. Neglect depth and inclination factors.

The base, 6.5 ft by 9.75 ft in plan, has its underside 4.5 ft down. Tests were run on the medium dense clean sand with φ′ = 32°; it weighs 115 pcf moist and 123 pcf saturated. Use the Brinch Hansen shape set on B′/L, s_q = (B′ sin φ′)/L + 1; s_γ = 1 − 0.4 × (B′/L), together with N_γ = (N_q − 1) × 1.5 tan φ′. Neglect depth and inclination factors.

The ground is a saturated medium stiff clay weighing 18.8 kN/m³, with s_u 940 psf. The clay cannot drain while the load goes on.

Column load 590 kN. Its square footing is 2.4 m on a side. Required net FS: 3. A trial design founds it at 1.1 m. The block of concrete, 24 kN/m³, rises from the base to grade. The net FS is the net capacity over the net applied pressure P/B² + D(24 − γ), the concrete replacing the clay (kPa). Undrained, φ = 0: the net capacity q_ult − γD = 5.14 s_c d_c s_u with a Meyerhof s_c of 1 + 0.2(B/L); apply the Brinch Hansen (1970) depth factors: d_c: 1 + 0.4 (D/B) if D/B ≤ 1, otherwise 1 + 0.4 × tan⁻¹(D/B).

Find the smallest depth D_required (m) that meets the required net FS, and FS_at_D for the depth on the drawings. Neglect inclination factors.

Treat the clay as undrained during loading. The ground is a saturated medium stiff clay (s_u 980 psf in quick tests; γ 18.9 kN/m³).

Design load from the column: 530 kN. Its square footing is 1.9 m on a side. Bearing must give FS_net ≥ 2.5. A trial design founds it at 2.2 m. Concrete at 24 kN/m³ is poured from the base up to the surface.

Neglect inclination factors. Short-term (φ = 0): use the net capacity 5.14 s_c d_c s_u, s_c = 1.2 for the square (1 + 0.2 B/L); apply the Brinch Hansen (1970) depth factors, d_c of 1 + 0.4 D/B (D ≤ B), switching to 1 + 0.4 tan⁻¹(D/B) (D > B). Net FS = net capacity divided by the net applied pressure, P over B² plus D times (24 − γ), both in kPa. Determine the smallest depth D_required (m) that meets the required net FS, together with FS_at_D, the net FS of the drawn design.

The structural engineer quotes 360 kN for this column. It stands on a square base of side 1.8 m. A uniform medium stiff clay extends well below the base whose undrained shear strength is 900 psf and γ 18.3 kN/m³. Required net FS: 3. The tender drawings give 1.3 m of embedment. The block of concrete, 24 kN/m³, rises from the base to grade. The column is loaded before any consolidation can occur.

Net FS = net capacity divided by the net applied pressure (column load / B²) + (24 − γ) × D (kPa). With φ = 0 the net capacity, 5.14 × s_c × d_c × s_u governs, s_c = 1 + 0.2 × B/L = 1.2; apply the Brinch Hansen (1970) depth factors, d_c = 1 + 2D/(5B) for D/B up to 1, else 1 + 0.4 arctan(D/B). Neglect inclination factors.

What are D_required, the smallest embedment in m at which the net FS reaches the requirement, and the net FS_at_D of the trial depth?

Required: D_required, the shallowest depth meeting the net FS (m), together with FS_at_D, the net FS of the drawn design. Net FS = net capacity divided by the net applied pressure P/B² + D(24 − γ), the concrete replacing the clay. With φ = 0 the net capacity, the gross value less γD, which is 5.14 s_u s_c d_c governs and s_c = 1 + 0.2 B/L, i.e. 1.2 here; apply the Brinch Hansen (1970) depth factors, d_c = 1 + 2D/(5B) for D/B up to 1, else 1 + 0.4 arctan(D/B).

Beneath the footing lies medium stiff clay (s_u 810 psf in quick tests; γ 18 kN/m³). Loading is quick; the check is undrained. Column load 550 kN. Plan size is fixed at 2.2 m square. The owner asks for a net safety factor of 2.5. So far the base is detailed at 1.7 m depth. The block of concrete, 24 kN/m³, rises from the base to grade. Neglect inclination factors.

Divide it by the net applied pressure P/B² + D(24 − γ), the concrete replacing the clay (kPa). Undrained, φ = 0: use the net capacity, 5.14 × s_c × d_c × s_u with Meyerhof's s_c = 1 + 0.2(B/L); apply the Brinch Hansen (1970) depth factors: d_c = 1 + 0.4 D/B up to D/B = 1, then 1 + 0.4 tan⁻¹(D/B). Neglect inclination factors.

Design load from the column: 460 kN. It stands on a square base of side 2.1 m. Construction is fast compared with consolidation, so the short-term check governs. Compute the least founding depth D_required in m that gives the required net FS, together with FS_at_D, the net FS of the drawn design.

With φ = 0 take the net capacity q_ult − γD = 5.14 s_c d_c s_u where s_c = 1.2 for the square (1 + 0.2 B/L); apply the Brinch Hansen (1970) depth factors: d_c equal to 1 + 0.4(D/B) when D/B ≤ 1 and to 1 + 0.4 arctan(D/B) when D/B > 1.

The ground is a saturated medium stiff clay of bulk unit weight 19.2 kN/m³ and undrained strength 920 psf. The clay cannot drain while the load goes on. To get FS_net, scale it by the inverse of the net applied pressure (P/B² + (24 − γ)D), both in kPa.

Find D_required (m), the first depth at which FS_net reaches its target, plus FS_at_D at the depth now shown. Neglect inclination factors.
